unitDescription.value: In this unit, students explore commercial design by examining how products are developed to meet user needs and succeed in competitive markets. Students investigate market analysis, target audiences, product design and manufacturing processes, and basic business principles such as value proposition, cost, and sustainability. Through analysis of existing commercial products and innovation case studies, students develop an understanding of how designers balance functionality, aesthetics, ethical considerations, and commercial viability. The unit emphasises innovation, enterprise skills, and informed decision-making in the development of market-ready designed solutions.

description.value: In this assessment, students complete an examination that assesses their understanding of key commercial design principles. The exam includes questions on how designers analyse needs and opportunities, consider ethical and sustainability factors, and apply innovation and enterprise skills when developing commercial products. Students demonstrate knowledge of materials, systems, and manufacturing considerations, as well as basic business concepts such as target audiences, market needs, and value creation. This assessment focuses on students’ ability to explain and apply foundational commercial design knowledge to authentic product design contexts.

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 10 students explain how people consider factors that impact on design decisions and the technologies used to design and produce products, services and environments for sustainable living. They explain the contribution of innovation, enterprise skills and emerging technologies to global preferred futures. For one or more of the technologies contexts, students explain the features of technologies and their appropriateness for purpose, and create designed solutions based on an analysis of needs or opportunities. Students create, adapt and refine design ideas, processes and solutions and justify their decisions against developed design criteria that include sustainability. They communicate design ideas, processes and solutions to a range of audiences, including using digital tools. Students independently and collaboratively develop and apply production and project management plans, adjusting processes when necessary. They select and use technologies skilfully and safely to produce designed solutions.

description.value: In this assessment, students respond to a given design situation by developing a commercial product for a specified target audience. Students communicate their final designed solution through appropriate representations and justify their decisions, demonstrating innovation, enterprise skills, and effective use of technologies throughout the design process.

keyTeachingExperiences.value:
Theory: Introduction to the principles of commercial design and the role of the industrial designer in a market-driven economy. Exploration of market context, including the distinction between niche and mass-market products. Discussion on how economic, social, and environmental factors influence the success of a designed solution within a specific marketplace.

They select a common household product and identify its market position, competitors, and the specific problem it was designed to solve. Students begin a digital design journal to document market observations and initial insights into commercial viability.

lessons.title: Introduction to Commercial Design
lessons.learningGoal: Define the core principles of commercial design and explain the role of industrial designers in a market-driven economy.

orientate.smartStart: List three manufactured products you used before arriving at St Brendan's College this morning and identify the specific problem each was manufactured to solve.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can define commercial design principles and explain the role of industrial designers in a market economy

activities.title: Core Commercial Design Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce foundational commercial design vocabulary explicitly on the whiteboard. Explain how an industrial designer operates at the intersection of aesthetic appeal, ergonomic functionality, and manufacturing economics. Model how commercial viability dictates whether a concept moves from prototype to factory floor. For example, explain that a beautifully designed chair cannot succeed commercially if the injection-moulding tooling costs exceed projected sales revenue.
activities.studentsDo: Read the three key terms in the workbook table and match each term to its correct definition from the scrambled definition bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each commercial design term in the table to its correct definition using the provided definition bank.
activities.questioning:
q: Why is commercial viability just as critical as aesthetics when designing a manufactured product?
Expected: A product must cover tooling and production costs and return a profit to survive commercially.
q: How does an industrial designer differ from a craft artisan?
Expected: Industrial designers design for mass production, assembly lines, and broad consumer usability rather than one-off bespoke pieces.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions in bank: 'The professional practice of designing products for mass production, ergonomics, and aesthetic appeal.', 'The ability of a product to generate sufficient commercial revenue to exceed production and distribution costs.', 'A focused, targeted segment of a broader market defined by specialised consumer needs.'
activities.eLearning: Ensure workbooks are open; display the terminology reference slide on the main screen.
activities.transition: Link these definitions directly to the upcoming guided notes on market context and consumer scale.

activities.title: Commercial Context Guided Notes
activities.teacherDoes: Deliver direct instruction on how commercial designers balance economic, social, and environmental constraints. Contrast high-volume mass-market commodities against low-volume niche innovations. Read the cloze statements aloud, pausing before each key concept to emphasise how unit cost declines as production volume increases. Model how to use context clues within the sentence structure to select the correct term from the word bank.
activities.studentsDo: Listen to the explicit instruction and fill in the missing terms in the cloze sentences using the provided word bank in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill in the missing terms in your workbook cloze sentences as we analyse mass-market scale versus niche market specialization.
activities.questioning:
What economic advantage allows mass-market products to achieve lower retail prices? Expected: Economies of scale allow fixed tooling and manufacturing costs to be spread across thousands of units.
How do social and environmental factors alter commercial viability for modern Australian designers? Expected: Consumers demand recyclable materials and ethical production, meaning unsustainable products face consumer backlash and regulatory penalties.
activities.scaffolding: Word bank: consumer, niche, economic. Definition reminder: Mass-market = broad demographic appeal with standardized components. Niche market = targeted appeal for specific user groups.
activities.eLearning: Project the guided notes display on the whiteboard.
activities.transition: Prepare students to classify authentic physical products into market categories based on these principles.

activities.title: Market Context Classification
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the classification of commercial products based on production volume, unit price, and target audience breadth. Model with an everyday example: 'A mass-produced injection-moulded plastic ruler is manufactured in tens of thousands for school and office supply chains (mass-market). Conversely, a bespoke carbon-fibre racing paddle crafted for outrigger canoeists at Keppel Bay is produced in limited runs for athletes (niche).' Guide students to sort four specific products into their respective buckets.
activities.studentsDo: Classify the four items from the bank into either the Mass-Market or Niche Market bucket in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Sort each product from the bank into either the Mass-Market or Niche Market category bucket.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why is a standard two-slice household toaster categorized as a mass-market product?
expected: It is produced in massive volumes for general domestic households with standardized electrical specifications.
prompt: Why does custom orthopedic footwear belong in a niche market?
expected: It caters to specific biomechanical needs, has high production labor per unit, and targets a narrow demographic.
activities.scaffolding: Category rules: Mass-Market = high volume, standardized, retail chains. Niche Market = low volume, customized, specialist outlets.
activities.eLearning: Active circulation around the room to monitor classification accuracy.
activities.transition: Wrap up classification to consolidate findings into the Smart Finish 3-2-1 reflection.

lessons.title: Product Deconstruction and Market Mapping
lessons.learningGoal: Deconstruct a commercial product to identify its market position, competitor landscape, and core design problem.

orientate.smartStart: Inspect the reusable drink bottle on your desk. Write down the single most important design feature that makes someone choose it over a disposable single-use plastic bottle.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can deconstruct a product to identify its market position, competitors, and design problem

activities.title: Commercial Product Audit Modelling
activities.teacherDoes: Place a standard double-walled stainless-steel drink bottle under the document camera. Model an end-to-end commercial deconstruction audit: identify material selection (food-grade 304 stainless steel), manufacturing processes (hydroforming, powder-coating), ergonomic considerations (silicone seal, carry loop), and target market. Explain aloud how each technical decision addresses a consumer pain point while preserving commercial profitability.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the modelled audit and tick off each foundational audit criterion on the workbook checklist as the teacher verifies it.
activities.visibleInstructions: Follow the teacher's modelled product audit and tick off each verified commercial criterion on your audit checklist.
activities.questioning:
Why do manufacturers choose powder-coating over liquid enamel for portable drink bottles? Expected: Powder-coating provides higher impact resistance, better grip texture, and lower VOC emissions during mass production.
What consumer problem does a double-walled vacuum cavity solve compared to single-wall aluminium? Expected: It eliminates exterior condensation and prevents thermal transfer, keeping beverages cold in high temperatures.
activities.scaffolding: Audit criteria: Primary material & tooling method identified, core functional problem defined, two direct competitor brands named, commercial market position verified.
activities.eLearning: Laptops closed; document camera projected on main display.
activities.transition: Transition from observational auditing to collaborative market mapping of competing products.

workbookSpec.title: Product Deconstruction Audit Checklist
workbookSpec.prompt: Verify that a comprehensive commercial product audit includes all four critical technical and market criteria.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All four items checked: Primary materials and hydroforming/powder-coating tooling identified; core thermal insulation problem defined; direct competitors Yeti and Hydro Flask named; premium mass-market positioning verified.
items: Identify the primary manufacturing materials and production forming methods
Define the specific ergonomic or consumer problem the product solves
Name at least two direct competitor brands competing in the same category
Determine whether the product targets a mass-market or niche market segment

activities.teacherAnswerKey: All four criteria ticked. The modelled audit confirms stainless steel hydroforming, thermal insulation problem, competitors such as Yeti and Hydro Flask, and premium niche-to-mass retail positioning.

activities.title: Co-Constructed Market Matrix
activities.teacherDoes: Guide the class to evaluate three common household kettles across two critical commercial variables: Retail Price Tier (Low / Medium / High) and Functional Complexity (Basic / Advanced). Co-construct the matrix on the board, demonstrating how price and feature complexity dictate market positioning (e.g. Budget Mass-Market vs Premium Specialty). Model an entry for the class: 'For the Generic Plastic Kettle, we note a Low price tier and Basic functionality, which places it in the mass-market budget category.'
activities.studentsDo: Contribute to class discussion and record the price tier, functionality level, and market position for each kettle in the workbook table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the market matrix table by recording the price tier, functionality level, and market position for each sample product.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Where does a generic 2kW plastic kettle sit on a price-versus-functionality matrix?
expected: Low price tier, basic functionality, representing a budget mass-market position.
prompt: Why would a brand develop a digital variable-temperature kettle at triple the retail price?
expected: To capture a premium market segment (e.g., specialty tea and coffee enthusiasts) willing to pay for precise thermal control.
activities.scaffolding: Options for columns: Price Tier = Low / Medium / High; Functionality = Basic / Advanced; Market Position = Mass-market budget / Mass-market premium / Niche specialist.
activities.eLearning: Display the 2x2 Price vs Functionality quadrant on the classroom screen to support student spatial reasoning.
activities.transition: Direct students to apply this analysis independently to an everyday product of their choice.

activities.title: Independent Product Deconstruction Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Circulate and provide targeted feedback as students select an everyday commercial product (e.g. cordless drill, running shoe, mechanical pencil) and deconstruct its commercial justification. Prompt students to use formal design language: cost-benefit trade-offs, materials efficiency, and competitive differentiation. Model a quick audit on the whiteboard for a standard item like a refillable water bottle: state the product, the problem of single-use waste and thermal retention, and justify its mid-tier stainless steel market position.
activities.studentsDo: Independently complete the three sections of the product audit in the workbook: product identification, core problem solved, and market position justification using formal design terminology.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the independent product audit in your workbook: name your product, explain the core problem it solves, and justify its commercial market position using the provided sentence starter.
activities.questioning:
prompt: What primary trade-off did the manufacturer make between durability and retail price?
Expected: They selected lightweight composite polymers over machined metal to lower shipping weight and consumer retail cost.
prompt: How does your chosen product communicate its value proposition to the consumer on the retail shelf?
Expected: Packaging callouts emphasizing battery longevity, ergonomic rubber overmoulding, or extended warranty periods.
activities.scaffolding: Sentence starter for justification: 'This product occupies a [budget/premium/niche] market position because its [materials/features] specifically solve the problem of... at a price point that rivals cannot easily match.' Key vocabulary: market position, cost-benefit trade-off, competitive differentiation, material efficiency.
activities.eLearning: Students work independently in workbooks; roam the perimeter to check student entries.
activities.transition: Conclude independent audits and prepare to share findings during the Culminate phase.

lessons.title: Establishing the Digital Design Journal
lessons.learningGoal: Structure a professional design journal hierarchy to document market observations, competitor audits, and commercial insights.

orientate.smartStart: State two risks a commercial design firm faces if their design team fails to record primary research, user testing, and competitor pricing in an organized project journal.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can structure a professional design journal to document market observations and commercial insights

activities.title: Design Journal Information Architecture
activities.teacherDoes: Model the information architecture required for a professional commercial design journal on the projector. Show how professional designers structure their digital documentation into clear parent sections (Market Research, Product Deconstruction, Ideation) with nested child pages (Competitor Audit, Stakeholder Needs, Material Analysis). Emphasise that this tree structure ensures audit evidence is traceable during QCAA assessment.
activities.studentsDo: Study the modelled sitemap hierarchy in the workbook and complete the missing branches to establish a clear taxonomy for their design journal.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine the design journal sitemap in your workbook and complete the nested branches under Market Research and Product Deconstruction.
activities.questioning:
q: Why is a nested parent-child sitemap superior to keeping a flat list of journal notes?
Expected: It groups related technical and market research logically, allowing quick retrieval of specific commercial evidence.
q: Where would material durability tests and disassembly sketches be archived in this journal hierarchy?
Expected: Nested under the Product Deconstruction parent node.
activities.scaffolding: Hierarchy levels: Root = Design Journal Home; Parents = Market Research, Product Deconstruction; Children = Competitor Audit, Stakeholder Needs, Material Analysis, Functional Breakdown.
activities.eLearning: Laptops down while the teacher models the sitemap hierarchy on the projector screen.
activities.transition: Transition from overall folder and journal hierarchy to defining the specific quality standards needed for each entry.

activities.title: Journal Quality Criteria Verification
activities.teacherDoes: Co-construct the professional quality standards for design journal entries with the class. Display an unannotated snapshot of a commercial product alongside a fully annotated QCAA-standard journal entry featuring callouts for materials, ergonomic grip, and retail price comparison. Guide students through evaluating each standard on their checklist, explicitly demonstrating how to verify each requirement against the projected assessment standard.
activities.studentsDo: Collaboratively review the five design journal quality standards and verify each criterion in the workbook checklist by ticking off confirmed elements in their digital design journal layout.
activities.visibleInstructions: Review the co-constructed documentation criteria and tick off each verified standard in your workbook checklist to ensure your digital journal meets commercial presentation requirements.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why must every product image in a commercial design journal include technical callouts rather than just looking good?
expected: Annotations provide evidence of critical analysis regarding manufacturing constraints, material selection, and user interaction, which directly satisfies QCAA design criteria.
prompt: Why is recording dated entries important in commercial product development?
expected: It establishes intellectual property timelines, tracks project milestones, and provides clear chronological evidence of design iteration and decision-making.
activities.scaffolding: Checklist standards include: Chronological dated headings, annotated visual evidence, explicit link to target user demographic, evaluation of commercial constraints (cost/materials), and clear competitor pricing comparison.
activities.eLearning: Display the exemplar journal entry side-by-side with the interactive checklist on the main classroom screen.
activities.transition: Move from verifying quality criteria to drafting an authentic baseline market observation entry in the design journal.

activities.title: Baseline Market Observation Entry

Model the 3-2-1 response structure on the board: list three physical product/market observations, two distinct consumer characteristics, and one commercial viability reflection. Emphasize the use of QCAA design terminology, such as commercial viability, material selection, and target demographic.
activities.studentsDo: Draft the initial baseline design journal entry in the workbook using the structured 3-2-1 sections, incorporating specific local commercial examples.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete your baseline journal entry in your workbook using the 3-2-1 sections: 3 market observations, 2 consumer characteristics, and 1 commercial viability reflection.

activities.eLearning: Students open their digital design journal files or print workbooks to record the baseline entry; monitor progress across the room.

q: Under what design circumstances is direct observation superior to self-reported survey answers?
Expected: Users frequently misremember or fail to articulate unconscious physical workarounds and environmental habits that observation exposes.

activities.title: Survey Question Co-Construction
activities.teacherDoes: Guide the class through co-constructing three balanced, unbiased market research questions focused on campus amenities or community sports facilities (e.g. St Brendan's College sporting infrastructure or Yeppoon Seagulls community equipment). Model on the whiteboard how to transform a biased item ('Don't you love our new gym?') into an objective 5-point Likert scale ('Rate your level of satisfaction with current equipment availability: 1 = Very Dissatisfied to 5 = Very Satisfied'). Guide students to complete the demographic bracket, Likert scale, and open qualitative prompt in their workbook sections.

activities.visibleInstructions: Draft three structured market research questions in your workbook following the prompts: 1 demographic question, 1 five-point Likert scale question, and 1 open qualitative question.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why must demographic response options provide mutually exclusive, comprehensive age or role categories?
expected: Overlapping brackets (e.g. 15-18 and 18-21) confuse respondents and invalidate demographic data sorting.
prompt: Why is it essential to anchor both endpoints of a Likert scale with explicit labels?
expected: Without labelled endpoints (e.g. Strongly Disagree vs Strongly Agree), respondents interpret numerical values inconsistently.
activities.scaffolding:
Question structure checklist:
- Demographic: Mutually exclusive brackets (e.g. Under 14, 14–16, 17–18, Staff/Parent).
- Quantitative: Neutral stem + 5-point anchors (1 = Strongly Disagree, 2 = Disagree, 3 = Neutral, 4 = Agree, 5 = Strongly Agree).
- Qualitative: Non-leading stem ('Describe the single most frustrating aspect of using...').

activities.questioning:
What critical failure occurs if a design team distributes a digital survey before conducting a peer pilot test? Expected: Ambiguous wording, confusing scales, or technical glitches are distributed to the wider public, permanently corrupting the collected dataset.

activities.title: User Persona Anatomy Callout Mapping
activities.teacherDoes: Project a completed industrial User Persona archetype on the classroom screen (e.g. 'Marcus – Yeppoon Coastal Surf Lifesaver & Volunteer Equipment Officer'). Deconstruct the anatomy of the persona across four numbered callouts: (1) Demographic Baseline, (2) Psychographic Drivers & Lifestyle Values, (3) Operational Frustrations & Pain Points, and (4) Technical / Physical Environment Constraints. Model callout 1 and callout 2 explicitly on the board, demonstrating how research data directly informs persona characteristics rather than designer guesswork.

activities.questioning:
Why do commercial designers formulate a User Persona archetype rather than designing for a single real individual? Expected: Personas synthesise aggregate trends and common frustrations across an entire market segment, preventing idiosyncratic preferences from distorting the brief.
How do documented 'pain points' within a persona directly establish design opportunities? Expected: Every genuine pain point represents an unmet consumer need where an innovative designed solution can create commercial market demand.
activities.scaffolding:
Callout reference guide:
- Callout 1: Demographic Baseline (age, occupation, location, income band)
- Callout 2: Psychographic Motivations (core values, leisure priorities, attitudes)
- Callout 3: Operational Pain Points (physical barriers, equipment breakdown, wasted time)
- Callout 4: Environmental / Technical Constraints (operating conditions, durability demands, technology habits)

workbookSpec.title: User Persona Structural Anatomy
workbookSpec.prompt: Examine the projected User Persona reference figure and use the four numbered callouts to detail the design function of each quadrant.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
Callout 1: Demographic Baseline -> Establishes user age, location, occupation, and baseline financial resources to ensure the product is priced and positioned realistically.
Callout 2: Psychographic Motivations -> Maps lifestyle values, personal aspirations, and recreational priorities that dictate styling, brand alignment, and emotional appeal.
Callout 3: Operational Pain Points -> Identifies specific functional frustrations, equipment failures, and inefficiency that define the core design opportunity.
Callout 4: Technical & Environmental Constraints -> Details operating environments (e.g. saltwater exposure, UV, high impact) and device interactions that govern material selection and durability.

activities.title: User Story Requirement Framing
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through the Agile User Story framework: 'As a [user role], I want [specific feature or capability], so that [tangible commercial or functional benefit].' Model how to translate a pain point identified from Yeppoon Seagulls Rugby League equipment handling or Livingstone Shire Council recreational facilities into an actionable design brief requirement. Guide students to co-construct an exemplar on the board, demonstrating why vague 'so that' statements (e.g. 'so that it is good') fail commercial brief criteria.

activities.questioning:
question: Why must the 'so that' clause express an authentic user benefit rather than just repeating the feature?
Expected: The 'so that' clause establishes the commercial value proposition and proves that the requested feature solves an underlying consumer need.
question: What distinguishes a design requirement framed through a user story from an arbitrary aesthetic choice?
Expected: A user story roots the requirement in validated user roles and measurable functional outcomes rather than subjective designer taste.
activities.scaffolding:
User story structure:
- Role stem: 'As a...' (e.g. As a St Brendan's College boarding sports captain...)
- Feature stem: 'I want...' (e.g. I want a weather-resistant, ventilated modular locker bag...)
- Justification stem: 'so that...' (e.g. so that wet training gear dries quickly and does not contaminate school uniforms).

Theory: Examination of the ethical and environmental responsibilities of commercial designers. Introduction to Life Cycle Thinking (LCT) and the 'Cradle to Grave' vs. 'Cradle to Cradle' concepts. Discussion of ethical issues such as planned obsolescence and fair-trade manufacturing.

activities.title: Sustainability Vocabulary Matrix
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define key sustainability terminology including Life Cycle Thinking, Planned Obsolescence, Cradle-to-Grave, and Cradle-to-Cradle. Model examples using consumer electronics and packaging, demonstrating how linear models contrast with closed-loop biological and technical nutrient cycles. Direct students to complete the matching table in their workbooks using the definition bank.
activities.studentsDo: Match each locked sustainability term in column 1 to its corresponding definition from the definition bank provided below the table by writing the matching definition into the Match column.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each sustainability term in column 1 to its correct definition from the bank by writing the matching definition into the second column.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why do linear cradle-to-grave models inevitably lead to resource depletion in commercial design?
Expected: Because raw materials are extracted, processed, and ultimately disposed of in landfill without nutrient recovery.
prompt: How does a cradle-to-cradle framework redefine the concept of waste?
Expected: It treats all product outputs as technical or biological nutrients for new manufacturing cycles, completely eliminating landfill waste.
activities.scaffolding: Full definitions provided in bank: 1. Life Cycle Thinking: Considering all environmental impacts across extraction, manufacture, use, and end-of-life. 2. Planned Obsolescence: Deliberately designing products with a limited lifespan to force repeat purchases. 3. Cradle-to-Grave: A linear manufacturing model where materials end as landfill waste. 4. Cradle-to-Cradle: A regenerative closed-loop framework where all materials are perpetually cycled.
activities.eLearning: Keep laptops closed while completing physical workbook vocabulary tables.
activities.transition: Check answers as a cohort before moving to guided notes on manufacturing flow models.

activities.title: Guided Notes on Lifecycle Models
activities.teacherDoes: Model the contrast between linear extraction-use-disposal cycles and circular biological/technical loops using whiteboard schematics. Explain how virgin polymer extraction drives embodied energy while closed-loop systems preserve material value. For example, contrast single-use polyethylene packaging with modular, infinitely recyclable aluminium enclosures.
activities.studentsDo: Fill in the missing technical terms in the cloze sentences in your workbook using the provided word bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the cloze passage in your workbook by inserting the correct terms from the word bank into the numbered blanks.
activities.questioning:
q: Why might a commercial manufacturer choose a linear model despite high disposal costs?
expected: Lower upfront tooling and material procurement costs compared to establishing reverse logistics and recycling infrastructure.
q: What is the role of technical nutrients in a circular product lifecycle?
expected: Synthetic or metallic materials designed to be continually dismantled and remanufactured without loss of quality.
activities.scaffolding: Word bank: linear, circular, closed-loop, environmental. Full definitions displayed on the front board for reference: Linear economy (take-make-dispose), Circular economy (restorative and regenerative by design), Closed-loop (system where waste becomes input), Environmental degradation (deterioration of the environment through depletion of resources).
activities.eLearning: Engage with explicit whiteboard diagram explanations; record verified terms into the student workbook.
activities.transition: Transition directly into the structured generative reflection on consumer electronics lifecycles.

activities.title: Generative Reflection on Circular Barriers
activities.teacherDoes: Model how to write a QCAA-style analytical justification linking commercial design constraints (glued housings, proprietary screws) directly to material recovery barriers in consumer electronics. Explicitly demonstrate how to incorporate technical terms such as 'cross-contamination', 'non-destructive disassembly', and 'linear economic models' into structured written responses.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the three-part written reflection in your workbook analyzing commercial barriers, material challenges, and design modifications for consumer electronics.
activities.visibleInstructions: Write responses in the three designated sections of your workbook evaluating why electronics manufacturers face challenges shifting to circular design.
activities.questioning:
q: How do permanent adhesives in smartphone assemblies prevent circular material recovery?
Expected: Glued battery and screen housings prevent non-destructive disassembly, making component repair and clean material sorting economically unviable.
q: What design modification allows quick disassembly at end-of-life?
Expected: Standardised snap-fits or modular magnetic fasteners that release without damaging component substrates.
activities.scaffolding:
Section 1 starter: 'The primary commercial barrier is...' 
Section 2 starter: 'A key material challenge involves...' 
Section 3 starter: 'To improve recovery, designers should modify...'
activities.eLearning: Monitor student writing from the rear of the classroom, checking for specific technical vocabulary usage.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students with 1 minute remaining before the summary exit ticket.

workbookSpec.title: Generative Reflection on Circular Barriers
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate the commercial and material constraints of transitioning consumer electronics from linear to circular frameworks.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
1. High cost of manual disassembly and proprietary glued components prevent automated material recovery while sales models rely on frequent replacement cycles.
2. Micro-soldered rare earth elements and blended polymers cause chemical cross-contamination during shredding.
3. Implement modular assembly using standardised mechanical fasteners and snap-fits to enable rapid, non-destructive component harvesting.

activities.visibleInstructions: Match the ethical manufacturing terms in column 1 to their correct definitions from the bank below the table.
activities.questioning:
prompt: How does supply chain transparency protect consumers from corporate greenwashing?
Expected: It provides verifiable public data on raw material provenance, factory working conditions, and environmental compliance.
prompt: Why do commercial designers implement artificial software or hardware obsolescence?
Expected: To stimulate consumer demand cycles and guarantee ongoing repeat product sales.

Planned Obsolescence: Deliberately designing products with artificial lifespans or unserviceable parts to force replacement.

activities.title: Planned Obsolescence Case Study Analysis
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through an analysis of consumer electronics designed with sealed adhesive batteries and proprietary pentalobe fasteners. Model how to construct a critical evaluation connecting commercial profit motives to e-waste accumulation. Example: 'When examining sealed enclosures, we do not simply state it is hard to open; we analyse the deliberate trade-off between IP67 water resistance ratings and lifetime serviceability, noting how proprietary fastener systems restrict third-party repair access.'
activities.studentsDo: Read the case study stimulus in your workbook and complete the three analytical sections evaluating the mechanical failure point, economic driver, and ethical design alternative.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the three-part case study analysis in your workbook evaluating how non-replaceable components represent planned obsolescence.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the primary commercial justification given by manufacturers for gluing batteries inside devices?
expected: Enabling thinner device profiles, structural rigidity, and water resistance, despite severely compromising repairability.
question: How does this practice breach Australian consumer expectations of product durability?
expected: It forces premature disposal of functional electronics when only a single consumable component degraded.
activities.scaffolding: Section prompts guide students: Section 1 (Failure Mechanism), Section 2 (Commercial Rationale), Section 3 (Ethical Alternative). Terminology: sealed enclosure, adhesive bonding, modular repair, Right to Repair.
activities.eLearning: Workbooks only during analysis; ensure all students complete full sentence responses.
activities.transition: Transition from individual case study analysis into the commercial ethics classification task.

3. Incorporate standardised pull-tab adhesive strips or modular screw-secured battery brackets allowing certified third-party and consumer battery replacement.

activities.teacherDoes: Model the classification of commercial design practices into Ethical Practice versus Unethical Practice buckets, demonstrating how to evaluate supply chain claims against greenwashing criteria. For example, explain why publishing tier-one and tier-two factory audit results moves a brand beyond superficial marketing into verifiable ethical transparency, whereas restricting replacement spare parts to proprietary dealerships locks consumers into restrictive, resource-heavy ecosystems.

activities.visibleInstructions: Sort all four commercial practices from the bank into the Ethical Practice or Unethical Practice buckets in your workbook.

prompt: Why is publishing tier-one and tier-two factory audit results considered ethical practice?
expected: It establishes accountability and validates that fair labour and environmental standards are enforced across sub-contractors.
prompt: What distinguishes legitimate durability engineering from unethical obsolescence?
expected: Legitimate design optimises component life for the intended operating environment, whereas unethical obsolescence deliberately inserts weak points or software throttles.

lessons.title: Life Cycle Analysis Practical Investigation
lessons.learningGoal: Conduct a Life Cycle Analysis (LCA) on a commercial product to identify environmental hotspots and propose sustainable design modifications.

orientate.smartStart: Students retrieve and write the four sequential stages of a product lifecycle (Raw Material Extraction, Manufacturing, Distribution, End-of-Life Disposal) in their workbooks from memory.

activities.title: LCA Flowchart Modeling
activities.teacherDoes: Model the systematic Life Cycle Analysis of a single-use commercial product (e.g. standard takeaway coffee cup). Map each stage on the board, demonstrating where high embodied energy and landfill diversion decision branches occur. Explicitly show how to trace the material pathway from raw inputs to disposal.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the teacher demonstration and complete the sequential life cycle stages and decision pathway in your workbook flow diagram.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the sequential product life cycle flow diagram in your workbook, recording the stages and the end-of-life diversion branch.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why is the raw material extraction stage for single-use lined paperboard cups particularly energy-intensive?
Expected: Virgin chemical pulping and petroleum-based polyethylene film extrusion require high thermal and electrical energy inputs.
prompt: What occurs at the end-of-life decision branch if municipal composting infrastructure is unavailable?
Expected: The composite cup cannot be separated by standard paper recycling streams, diverting it directly to general landfill waste.
activities.scaffolding: Stages: 1. Raw Material Extraction, 2. Manufacturing & Coating, 3. Transport & Retail Distribution, 4. Consumer Use & Disposal. Decision branch: Industrial Composting vs General Landfill.
activities.eLearning: Demonstrate municipal waste streams using Livingstone Shire Council waste guidelines on the projector (https://www.livingstone.qld.gov.au/).
activities.transition: Transition from teacher modeling to the collaborative product audit checklist.

workbookSpec.title: Commercial Product LCA Flow
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete the sequential life cycle stages and evaluate the end-of-life recovery pathway for the modelled commercial product.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. Raw Material Extraction: Timber pulp & virgin polyethylene. 2. Manufacturing: Thermal lamination. 3. Transport: Freight. 4. Disposal: Waste sorting. Branch: Specialised facility vs standard stream.

stages.label: 1. Raw Material Extraction (Timber pulp & virgin polyethylene)

rejoin.label: Evaluate redesign opportunities to eliminate composite linings.

activities.workbookMaterials: LCA Flowchart template and decision pathway in workbook.
activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. Raw Material Extraction: Bauxite/timber logging and petrochemical extraction for polymer lining.
2. Manufacturing: High-heat Kraft pulping, sheet forming, and polyethylene thermal lamination.
3. Transport: Global and regional road freight.
4. Consumer Disposal: Branch evaluation where lack of specialized hydrapulping results in 100% landfill diversion.

activities.title: Co-Constructed Product Hotspot Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Guide the class through a collaborative environmental audit of a standard commercial school backpack. Model how to interrogate material composition labels and supply chain pathways, explicitly linking each checkpoint to Life Cycle Thinking (LCT) principles. Demonstrate how to verify whether a material extraction point or manufacturing process constitutes an environmental hotspot according to QCAA Design standards.
activities.studentsDo: Audit the commercial backpack against the criteria in your workbook checklist, ticking each identified environmental hotspot verified during the co-constructed analysis.
activities.visibleInstructions: Review the backpack LCA criteria and tick the verified environmental hotspot boxes in your workbook checklist.
activities.questioning:
question: Why are blended synthetic fabrics (such as polyester bonded to PVC backing) classified as a severe end-of-life hotspot?
expected: Thermoset adhesives and mixed polymer types cannot be re-melted together without catastrophic loss of mechanical properties, preventing closed-loop recycling.
question: How does single-use polybag retail packaging contribute to the product's overall carbon footprint?
expected: It adds embodied fossil fuel extraction, energy-intensive polymer synthesis, and immediate post-retail municipal waste without adding functional product durability.
activities.scaffolding: Checklist criteria pre-populated: Virgin petrochemical nylon/polyester extraction (high embodied energy), Toxic PVC waterproofing backing (chlorine-based emissions), Global multi-leg container freight (heavy bunker fuel consumption), Non-separable mixed-material construction preventing textile recycling.
activities.eLearning: Display sample backpack material technical data sheets on screen while students complete physical checklist.
activities.transition: Move directly into independent green material alternative proposals.

workbookSpec.title: Backpack LCA Environmental Hotspot Checklist
workbookSpec.prompt: Tick the verified environmental impact hotspots identified during the co-constructed commercial backpack audit.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All four items must be ticked as verified environmental hotspots: virgin petroleum polymers, toxic PVC coating, multi-stage freight footprint, and unrecyclable mixed synthetic construction.
items: Primary outer shell uses virgin petroleum-derived nylon/polyester fabric
Waterproof backing relies on non-recyclable PVC coating
High transport carbon footprint from multi-stage international freight routes
Glued seams and mixed synthetic trims prevent non-destructive end-of-life material separation

activities.teacherAnswerKey: All four items must be verified and ticked by students: (1) Primary outer shell uses virgin petroleum-derived nylon/polyester fabric; (2) Waterproof backing relies on non-recyclable PVC coating; (3) High transport carbon footprint from multi-stage international freight routes; (4) Glued seams and mixed synthetic trims prevent non-destructive end-of-life material separation. These represent critical 'Cradle to Grave' linear model failures.

activities.title: Independent Green Alternative Proposal
activities.teacherDoes: Instruct students to select a commercial product, identify its critical environmental hotspot, and write a rigorous justification proposing a green material or structural alternative that preserves commercial viability. Model an example on the board for a portable speaker: replacing virgin ABS plastic with 100% ocean-bound recycled HDPE, noting how textured injection moulding masks the recycled polymer's natural color variance while maintaining drop-test impact resistance.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the structured written proposal in your workbook by specifying your chosen product, stating the green alternative, and justifying how consumer appeal and performance are maintained.
activities.visibleInstructions: Write your green alternative proposal in the three structured sections of your workbook, ensuring you provide a rigorous commercial and environmental justification.
activities.questioning: How does substituting virgin nylon with Global Recycled Standard (GRS) certified rPET maintain consumer appeal? Expected: It delivers identical tensile strength, abrasion resistance, and water repellency while providing an authentic eco-marketing claim. What manufacturing trade-off must designers manage when replacing solvent adhesives with mechanical ultrasonic welding? Expected: Higher initial capital tooling cost offset by faster cycle times and elimination of hazardous volatile organic compounds.
activities.scaffolding: Sentence starter provided: 'To improve sustainability without compromising commercial appeal, the product should replace [virgin material] with [green alternative], ensuring that [performance requirement] is maintained.' Key definitions available on the board: Embodied energy, cradle-to-cradle, environmental hotspot, circular economy.
activities.eLearning: Circulate rear of room to review written justifications for commercial feasibility and LCA alignment. Refer students needing digital sourcing data to Livingstone Shire Council or manufacturer sustainability reports.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students with 1 minute remaining before collecting workbooks and concluding the lesson.

workbookSpec.title: Green Alternative Proposal
workbookSpec.prompt: Propose a sustainable material modification for a commercial product, justifying how commercial appeal and performance are maintained.
workbookSpec.starter: To improve sustainability without compromising commercial appeal, the product should replace...

sections.label: 1. Identified commercial product and primary environmental hotspot
2. Proposed green material or structural alternative
3. Commercial justification (balancing durability, cost, and aesthetics)

activities.workbookMaterials: Green Alternative Proposal section in workbook.
activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. Commercial product: Insulated stainless steel drink bottle with virgin silicone gasket and single-use packaging hotspot.
2. Green alternative: 90% post-consumer recycled stainless steel body with food-grade thermoplastic elastomer (TPE) gasket and FSC-certified cardboard packaging.
3. Justification: Recycled stainless steel retains identical thermal insulation performance, corrosion resistance, and tactile appeal while reducing embodied carbon by 70%. TPE gaskets offer equal sealing performance while allowing standard thermal recycling.

activities.title: Manufacturing Processes Technical Definitions
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define the three core industrial manufacturing processes: Injection Moulding, CNC Machining, and Additive Manufacturing. activities.questioning:
prompt: Why is CNC machining classified as a subtractive process?
Expected: It cuts away unwanted material from a solid block or billet to achieve the final required geometry.
prompt: Why does injection moulding require high production volumes to be economically viable?
Expected: The initial cost of designing and fabricating precision steel tooling dies is extremely high and must be amortised over tens of thousands of manufactured units.
activities.scaffolding:
Core definitions to record:
1. Injection Moulding: A formative process where molten thermoplastic is injected under high pressure into a hardened steel mould cavity.
2. CNC Machining: A subtractive process using computer numerical control to guide rotary cutting tools that remove material from a solid billet.
3. Additive Manufacturing: A process of building three-dimensional parts layer-by-layer directly from digital CAD data.

activities.title: CAD Manufacturing Constraint Verification
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students on the main projector through applying manufacturing constraints to a 3D component model in CAD. Model how to inspect wall thickness uniformity, apply a mandatory 2-degree draft angle to vertical faces to ensure mould release, and identify and eliminate undercut geometry. Demonstrate the use of the section analysis tool to prove that wall thickness remains constant at 3.0 mm across complex geometry.

activities.questioning:
q: What is the primary function of adding a 2-degree draft angle to vertical walls in a CAD mould model?
Expected: It allows the solidified polymer part to eject cleanly from the metal mould cavity without friction, sticking, or surface scratching.
q: What defect occurs during injection moulding if wall thickness varies drastically across a component?
Expected: Thick sections cool slower than thin sections, leading to internal stresses, sink marks, and part warping.
activities.scaffolding:
Manufacturing constraint rules to verify in CAD:
1. Uniform wall thickness: set nominal wall to 3.0 mm across all sections.
2. Draft angle: minimum 2.0° applied to all vertical draw surfaces.
3. Undercuts: all interior ribs oriented parallel to the mould opening direction.

activities.title: Core Commercial Differentiation Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly present four commercial design concepts on the main board: Value Proposition, Market Saliency, Product Differentiation, and Competitive Advantage. Contrast a generic consumer product (e.g., an unbranded white plastic toaster) with an innovative market entrant. Model how distinct consumer pain points are solved through deliberate design decisions rather than cosmetic styling. Rear-of-room visual check to confirm active listening before student writing commences.

activities.visibleInstructions: Match each commercial term in Column 1 with its corresponding definition from the word bank by writing the matching definition in Column 2.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is differentiation critical when entering a saturated market?
expected: In a saturated market, multiple competitors offer identical core utility, so differentiation gives consumers a distinct reason to buy your product.
question: What distinguishes a genuine value proposition from an advertising slogan?
expected: An advertising slogan is a catchy phrase, whereas a value proposition is a measurable promise of functional, economic, or emotional value delivered.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
1. Value Proposition: A clear statement describing the tangible benefits a product provides, solving specific customer problems better than competitors.
2. Product Differentiation: The design and functional distinctions that set a product apart from competing alternatives.
3. Market Saliency: The degree to which a brand or product is prominent, memorable, and readily noticed by target consumers.
4. Competitive Advantage: A superior business or design condition that allows an enterprise to generate greater consumer demand or higher profit margins.
activities.eLearning: Project the definitions clearly on the whiteboard; ensure laptops remain closed during the explicit terminology delivery.

Value Proposition Components:

- Viability Measure: The quantifiable outcome (e.g. saves 15 minutes, reduces weight by 30%).

activities.title: Manufacturing Cost Structures Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Direct explicit teaching on the board: introduce Cost of Goods Sold (COGS), Fixed Overhead Costs, Variable Manufacturing Costs, and Economies of Scale. Use a local Yeppoon marine fabrication workshop context (e.g. Keppel Bay Marina repair facility). Model how purchasing aluminium sheet in bulk lowers raw material unit costs, while factory lease remains static regardless of whether 5 or 50 vessels are serviced. Check workbook engagement from the rear of the classroom.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the matching table in the workbook by pairing each financial term in Column 1 with its precise commercial definition from the provided definition bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each financial cost term in Column 1 to its exact definition from the definition bank by recording it in Column 2.
activities.questioning:
q: Why are direct labour hours classified under COGS rather than fixed administrative costs?
Expected: Direct labour is directly expended to fabricate each individual unit, so if production stops, direct labour costs cease.
q: How do high fixed costs influence the break-even volume of a new product?
Expected: High fixed costs require an enterprise to sell a significantly larger volume of units before total revenue surpasses total expenditure.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
1. Cost of Goods Sold (COGS): The direct costs directly attributable to the physical production of each unit (raw materials, machining time, direct assembly labour).
2. Fixed Costs: Overhead expenses that remain unchanged regardless of the volume of units manufactured (rent, equipment leases, building insurance).
3. Variable Costs: Expenses that fluctuate in direct proportion to the volume of units produced (raw polymers, fasteners, packaging, direct freight).
4. Economies of Scale: The commercial phenomenon where increasing production volume reduces the average cost per individual unit due to spreading fixed overheads and bulk purchasing discounts.
activities.eLearning: Keep laptops closed; display the financial cost formulas and definitions on the interactive screen.
activities.transition: Transition from definitions to numerical calculations of unit costs and volume scaling.

activities.title: Unit Cost and Economies of Scale Calculations
activities.teacherDoes: Model the core unit cost equation on the board: Unit Cost = (Total Fixed Costs / Volume) + Variable Cost per Unit. Walk students through a worked industrial batch scenario: A production run of an injection-moulded polypropylene equipment handle. Scenario A: Volume = 500 units, Fixed Mould Tooling = $5,000, Variable Polymer + Labour = $4.00/unit. Unit Cost = ($5,000 / 500) + $4.00 = $10.00 + $4.00 = $14.00. Scenario B: Volume = 5,000 units, Fixed Mould Tooling = $5,000, Variable Material = $3.50/unit (bulk discount). Unit Cost = ($5,000 / 5,000) + $3.50 = $1.00 + $3.50 = $4.50. Emphasise how tooling amortisation drives viability.
activities.studentsDo: Calculate unit costs across the two production volume batches in Section 1 of the workbook, then write the comparative analysis explaining how scale altered the unit economics in Section 2.
activities.visibleInstructions: Calculate the unit manufacturing costs for Batch A (500 units) and Batch B (5,000 units) in the Calculation Workspace, then answer the analysis prompt on economies of scale.
activities.questioning: Why did the fixed tooling cost per unit drop from $10.00 to $1.00 when batch volume multiplied by ten? Expected: The total fixed cost of $5,000 remained constant, so spreading it over 5,000 units divided the overhead burden across ten times as many products. If retail price is fixed at $20.00, how does batch size affect gross profit margin? Expected: Batch A produces $6.00 profit per unit (30% margin), whereas Batch B produces $15.50 profit per unit (77.5% margin), making the enterprise commercially viable.
activities.scaffolding:
Formulas provided:
1. Total Fixed Overhead = $5,000
2. Fixed Cost per Unit = Total Fixed Overhead / Total Units Produced
3. Total Unit Cost = Fixed Cost per Unit + Variable Cost per Unit
4. Gross Margin ($) = Target Retail Price - Total Unit Cost
activities.eLearning: Calculators permitted; keep web browsers closed during calculation practice.
activities.transition: Check student answers around the room; signal 2 minutes until we evaluate commercial viability on a continuum.

workbookSpec.title: Unit Cost and Scaling Analysis
workbookSpec.prompt: Calculate unit production costs across both batch scenarios and analyse the commercial impact of economies of scale.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
Section 1 Working:
Batch A: Fixed cost per unit = $5,000 / 500 = $10.00. Unit Cost = $10.00 + $4.00 = $14.00 per unit.
Batch B: Fixed cost per unit = $5,000 / 5,000 = $1.00. Unit Cost = $1.00 + $3.50 = $4.50 per unit.
Section 2 Analysis:
Increasing production tenfold reduced the total unit cost from $14.00 to $4.50 (a 67.8% decrease). This demonstrates economies of scale because fixed capital tooling costs are amortised over a high production run, enabling higher profit margins or competitive retail price reductions.

activities.title: Evaluating Commercial Product Viability
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the Product Economic Viability Scale (1 = Unviable / Negative Gross Margin to 5 = Highly Viable / Scalable with >60% Gross Margin). Present a commercial scenario: A designer produces custom recycled HDPE plastic fins for surfboards sold at Keppel Bay Marina. Retail price = $80. COGS = $55 (high manual CNC labour + low batch size). Factory fixed overhead per unit = $20. Total unit cost = $75. Net margin = $5 per set (6.25%). Model how to plot this scenario at 2 (Risky / Fragile Margin) due to vulnerability to material price spikes.
activities.studentsDo: Plot the three commercial manufacturing scenarios onto the continuum scale in the workbook and write a two-sentence justification for each rating based on unit cost, overhead exposure, and profit margin.
activities.visibleInstructions: Rate the economic viability of the three product manufacturing scenarios on the 1–5 scale. Write a concise justification beneath each scale citing unit costs and profit margins.
activities.questioning: Why is a product with high sales volume still rated as unviable (1 or 2) if variable costs are 90% of retail price? Expected: Any slight inflation in materials, freight, or labour will turn gross profit into a net financial loss. What operational adjustment could shift a product from a 2 rating to a 4 rating? Expected: Investing in automated production tooling to decrease manual labor time or increasing batch size to capture volume material discounts.
activities.scaffolding:
Continuum Scale Guide:
1: Unviable (Costs exceed retail price / loss-maker)
2: High Risk (0-15% margin; highly vulnerable to supply chain fluctuations)
3: Sustainable (16-35% margin; covers overheads but low reserve capital)
4: Commercially Viable (36-55% margin; solid reinvestment capability)
5: Highly Scalable (>55% margin; strong economies of scale)
activities.eLearning: Display the three manufacturing scenario profiles clearly on the board.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students that workbooks will be reviewed as we move into the Culminate phase.

activities.title: Appliance Feature Deconstruction and Cost Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly demonstrate deconstructing an electric benchtop kettle on the teacher workbench. Examine the four major subsystems: deep-drawn stainless steel vessel, injection-moulded polypropylene handle/base assembly, bi-metallic thermal cut-off sensor, and electrical wiring assembly complying with AS/NZS 3112 standards. Model ticking the checklist items in the workbook and show how to estimate raw COGS ($14.50) against a standard retail price ($49.00), demonstrating a 70% gross retail margin. Rear-of-room monitoring of active student tracking.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the modelled deconstruction, inspect the physical appliance features, and complete the manufacturing feature audit checklist in their workbooks by checking each subsystem and recording the estimated cost classification.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the appliance feature audit by ticking each manufacturing subsystem present on the inspected product and confirming compliance and cost drivers.
activities.questioning: Why does an injection-moulded polymer base cost significantly less per unit than a deep-drawn stainless steel container body? Expected: Polymer resin has lower raw material costs and rapid multi-cavity cycle times, whereas stainless steel requires multi-stage mechanical stamping and finishing. What risks does a designer face if they omit AS/NZS compliance fittings during initial cost modelling? Expected: The product cannot be legally sold in Australia, and retrofitting compliance electronics later causes major redesign and re-tooling costs.
activities.scaffolding:
Audit Subsystems:
1. External Enclosure (Polymer injection moulding vs. stamped metal alloy)
2. Primary Thermal/Mechanical Subsystem (Heating element, thermostat, contact pins)
3. Ergonomic / User Touchpoints (Over-moulded rubber grips, mechanical toggle latches)
4. Regulatory Safety Compliance (Thermal auto-fuse, insulated three-pin plug, earthing lead)

activities.title: Mapping Value Delivery on the Business Model Canvas
activities.teacherDoes: Co-construct a Business Model Canvas (BMC) focused on the three core pillars: Customer Segments, Value Propositions, and Revenue Streams. Use a regional commercial venture as the co-construction case study: Keppel Bay Marina's marine vessel equipment and support services (referencing stimulus website). Model how to write a precise customer segment and link it to an economic value proposition. Guide students through the prompts: 'Who is the paying customer segment? What exact problem does the service resolve? How is recurring revenue generated?' Direct students to complete the BMC audit table in their workbooks using the co-constructed examples.
activities.studentsDo: Work collaboratively with teacher guidance to populate the Business Model Canvas table in the workbook, mapping Customer Segments to specific Value Propositions and defining the resulting Revenue Streams, then ticking the audit confirmation column.
activities.visibleInstructions: Populate the Business Model Canvas table in your workbook. For each pillar, write the specific details co-constructed in class and check the audit confirmation column.
activities.questioning:
prompt: How does defining a precise customer segment alter the value proposition of a marine product?
Expected: Commercial fishing operators prioritise rugged durability and rapid servicing, whereas weekend recreational boaters prioritise ease of operation and aesthetic finish.
prompt: Why is it dangerous to list a product feature rather than a customer benefit under Value Propositions?
Expected: Customers pay for the solution to their problem (e.g. vessel security, saved maintenance time), not merely a feature (e.g. zinc-plated steel).

activities.title: Commercial Viability Synthesis and Defense
activities.teacherDoes: Set up independent synthesis task. Instruct students to synthesise findings from the physical appliance audit and the Business Model Canvas exercise. activities.title: Commercial Design Terminology Match
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the revision sequence by framing precise QCAA terminology as essential for top-band exam justifications. Explicitly model: 'Never write a product is cheap; write that it achieves cost-efficiency through optimised Cost of Goods Sold (COGS).' Direct attention to the matching grid in the printed workbooks.

activities.visibleInstructions: Match each commercial design term (1–5) to its correct definition (A–E) using the definition bank. Write the letter in the Match column.
activities.questioning:
Why is it vital to distinguish between fixed and variable costs when calculating the economic viability of a product? Expected: Fixed costs remain constant regardless of production volume, while variable costs fluctuate per unit. Both must be covered to calculate unit margins and set viable retail pricing.
How does psychographic data alter a design's value proposition compared to demographic data alone? Expected: Demographics only define who buys (age, income), whereas psychographics define why they buy (values, lifestyle preferences), enabling tailored functional and aesthetic design choices.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
- COGS: Direct costs attributable to the production of the goods sold.
- Planned Obsolescence: Designing a product with an artificially limited useful life to encourage repeat purchase.
- Value Proposition: The explicit statement of functional, aesthetic, or social benefits delivered to consumers.
- Demographic: Quantifiable statistical data of a population (age, income, location).
- Psychographic: Qualitative attributes relating to personality, lifestyle, values, and attitudes.

activities.title: I Do: Modelling the Justification Structure
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the 3-part justification structure: (1) Claim (identify design decision/principle), (2) Contextual Evidence (quote specific client/audience constraints), and (3) Commercial Impact (link to economic viability, user conversion, or brand equity). activities.questioning:
q: Why does an answer that only states 'aluminium is rust-proof' receive only low-band marks?
Expected: It merely describes a physical material property without connecting it to the client's financial constraints or long-term commercial lifecycle viability.
q: How does citing the coastal environmental conditions of Livingstone Shire Council strengthen the justification?
Expected: It demonstrates contextual analysis by showing why the selected material is appropriate for high-salinity exposure, preventing costly premature replacement.
activities.scaffolding:
Justification Framework:
- Claim: State design decision and principle (e.g. marine-grade 316 stainless steel with powder coating).
- Evidence: Cite brief requirements (e.g. high-salinity marine environment, heavy public pedestrian traffic).
- Commercial Impact: Explain commercial outcome (e.g. minimises recurring council maintenance expenditure, maximising lifecycle return on investment).

activities.questioning:
What is the critical production threshold that makes injection moulding viable despite massive tooling costs? Expected: High production volumes (economies of scale), where the high upfront tooling cost is amortised across tens of thousands of units, resulting in cents per unit.
What would occur to commercial viability if 3D printing were selected for 50,000 units? Expected: Production time would be prohibitively slow and per-unit material costs would remain flat, resulting in uncompetitive retail pricing and production bottlenecks.
activities.scaffolding:

- Injection Moulding: High initial tooling/die cost ($15,000+), rapid cycle times (seconds), very low per-unit variable cost ($0.15/unit).

workbookSpec.title: Independent Practice: Manufacturing Method Justification
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate and justify the selection of Injection Moulding versus 3D Printing for producing 50,000 units of a commercial reusable water bottle cap.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
1. Selection & Economies of Scale: For a production run of 50,000 units, the manufacturer must select injection moulding because the high production volume allows the significant initial capital tooling cost to be amortised across the entire run, achieving decisive economies of scale.
2. Comparative Cost & Commercial Impact: While 3D printing requires lower initial setup capital, its slow cycle times and high per-unit material costs make mass production commercially unviable. Injection moulding produces parts in seconds at a fraction of the unit cost, ensuring competitive retail pricing and sustainable profit margins.

activities.title: Innovation Strategy Definitions
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define the three commercial innovation strategies on the whiteboard: Incremental (continuous, low-risk enhancements to existing products), Radical (breakthrough technology applied to an established market), and Disruptive (simple or low-cost innovation creating a new value network that displaces market leaders). Direct students to the workbook vocabulary matching table.
activities.studentsDo: Read each term in the workbook table. Match each term to its correct definition using letters A, B, or C from the definition bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each innovation term to its correct definition from the bank below by writing the matching letter in the Match column.
activities.questioning:
Why might an established commercial firm prefer incremental innovation over disruptive innovation? Expected: Incremental innovation carries lower financial risk, protects existing customer revenue, and leverages current manufacturing tooling.
In what commercial scenario does a business face severe risk by only pursuing incremental innovation? Expected: When a competitor introduces a disruptive or radical technology that changes customer expectations or renders existing production lines obsolete.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
1. Incremental Innovation: Small, iterative improvements to existing products, materials, or features to retain market share.
2. Radical Innovation: Major technological breakthroughs that fundamentally change product architecture or function in an existing market.
3. Disruptive Innovation: New business models or accessible technologies that create a new market segment and displace established incumbents.
activities.eLearning: Laptops closed and eyes to the board during explicit definitions.
activities.transition: Check students' matched letters on the board, then move directly into applying these definitions to commercial case studies.

activities.title: SCAMPER Deconstruction
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the SCAMPER framework as a structured ideation tool for product pivoting. Model the 7 operations using an everyday stainless-steel water bottle: Substitute (bamboo fibre exterior), Combine (Bluetooth hydration sensor in base), Adapt (collapsible silicone bellows), Modify (oval cross-section for pocket fit), Put to another use (emergency camping lantern diffuser), Eliminate (threaded cap replaced with magnetic silicone seal), Reverse (fill from removable weighted base).
activities.studentsDo: Complete the cloze sentences in the workbook to capture the 7 operator definitions of the SCAMPER framework.
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill in the missing operational terms in the SCAMPER summary sentences using the word bank provided.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is 'Eliminate' often more commercially valuable than 'Combine' when redesigning consumer goods?
expected: Eliminating components reduces material costs, manufacturing steps, assembly time, and points of mechanical failure.
question: How does 'Adapt' differ from 'Substitute'?
expected: Substitute swaps out an existing material or component for another; Adapt alters a mechanism or concept borrowed from a different context to work here.
activities.scaffolding:
SCAMPER Operations:
- Substitute: Replace materials or parts.
- Combine: Integrate features or functions.
- Adapt: Borrow concepts from another context.
- Modify: Alter dimensions, shape, or scale.
- Put to another use: Target a completely new user purpose.
- Eliminate: Strip away non-essential elements.
- Reverse: Invert orientation, layout, or operational sequence.

activities.transition: Direct students to form assigned pairs to co-construct a product pivot on a familiar school product.

lessons.title: Enterprise Skills in Action: Rapid Sprint Challenge
lessons.learningGoal: Demonstrate enterprise skills including calculated risk-taking, collaboration, and adaptability in a time-constrained product design challenge.

orientate.smartStart: Rank the following 5 enterprise skills in your workbook from 1 (most vital for a design entrepreneur) to 5 (least vital): Collaboration, Calculated Risk-Taking, Adaptability, Rapid Prototyping, Effective Communication.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can apply enterprise skills to pivot a product design under time constraints

activities.title: Enterprise Skills Framework & Diagnostic
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly unpack the core enterprise skills required for commercial product design: Calculated Risk-taking (trialling novel materials or unproven configurations backed by functional logic), Collaboration (defining roles and negotiating team consensus under pressure), and Adaptability (pivoting product direction immediately when external constraints or client briefs shift). Model an example from Keppel Bay Marina: pivoting tourism operations when marine weather conditions change rapidly. Direct students to complete the checklist.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the enterprise skills self-audit checklist in the workbook by ticking their current baseline strength and highlighting their growth target for today's design sprint.
activities.visibleInstructions: Review the 5 enterprise skills in your checklist. Tick your strongest skill and identify the skill you will deliberately focus on during today's sprint challenge.
activities.questioning:
prompt: What distinguishes 'calculated risk-taking' from reckless guessing in commercial design?
expected: Calculated risk relies on user data, functional principles, and low-cost prototyping to test hypotheses before mass tooling.
prompt: Why is adaptability more critical than stick-to-the-plan execution in modern agile product teams?
expected: Market needs, supply chains, and consumer feedback change continuously; failing to adapt causes obsolete product launches.
activities.scaffolding:
Enterprise Skills Definitions:
1. Calculated Risk-taking: Willingness to experiment with unconventional forms, materials, or mechanisms backed by logic.
2. Collaboration: Structured role division, active listening, and collective accountability.
3. Adaptability: Immediate problem-solving response when design constraints change unexpectedly.
4. Rapid Communication: Concise visual and verbal articulation of concepts under deadlines.
5. Resourcefulness: Maximising value from constrained materials and limited tools.
activities.eLearning: Classroom timer active on projector; student laptops closed.
activities.transition: Form sprint teams of 3 and distribute the design scenario brief.

workbookSpec.title: Enterprise Skills Personal Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate your enterprise skill strengths and select your growth target for today's challenge.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Teacher verification that every student has selected a baseline capability and identified an explicit growth target for the upcoming sprint.
items: Calculated Risk-Taking: Testing novel materials, bold shapes, or unproven functional ideas

Adaptability: Pivoting design direction quickly when constraints change

Time Management: Delivering a finished concept within strict milestone limits

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Diagnostic self-assessment. Teacher verifies that each student has marked baseline strengths and a designated growth focus area for the sprint challenge.

activities.title: Rapid Sprint: The Cyclone Survival Kit Pivot
activities.teacherDoes: Launch the sprint: 'Teams have 15 minutes to conceptualise an emergency cyclone relief utility pack for Capricorn Coast households. Mid-way through, at minute 7, a constraint injection will occur.' Model sketching with 3 mandatory enterprise annotations: 'Point directly to a feature and write: [Skill: Adaptability - collapsible water pouch added when pack dimensions were halved].' At minute 7, announce the constraint injection: 'Material supply alert: All virgin plastics and primary batteries have been embargoed. You must pivot to mechanical/solar power and recycled cardboard/canvas construction.'
activities.studentsDo: In trios, sketch and annotate the rapid product concept in the workbook sketch space. Respond immediately to the minute 7 constraint injection by documenting a visible 'Pivot Point' on the sketch.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Sketch your emergency utility kit layout in the box. 2. Label Core Utility and Sustainable Materials. 3. When the mid-sprint constraint is announced, draw and label your 'Pivot Point'. 4. Annotate 3 specific enterprise skills applied.
activities.questioning:
q: How did your team resolve differing opinions when the material embargo was announced?
Expected: Team negotiated trade-offs by evaluating which solution maintained basic emergency survival functions.
q: Which enterprise skill enabled your team to modify your power generation system under time pressure?
Expected: Adaptability and resourcefulness allowed us to shift from battery power to a hand-crank dynamo.
activities.scaffolding:
Required Sketch Labels:
1. Core Utility Function (e.g., water purification, beacon, emergency storage)
2. Sustainable Material Choice (post-consumer recycled fabric, bamboo composite)
3. Mid-Point Pivot Point (the exact design change made following the constraint injection)
4. Annotations linking 3 features directly to Enterprise Skills (Risk-taking, Adaptability, Collaboration)
activities.eLearning: Projector displays 15-minute sprint clock with mid-point audible alert.
activities.transition: Stop sketching immediately when the sprint timer expires. Direct all students to open their reflection section.
