keyTeachingExperiences.value:
Theory: Introduction to formal graphical communication standards used to bridge the gap between design and manufacturing. Students examine the role of 3D visualisation in communicating complex design intent to stakeholders and investors. Explicit teaching covers Australian Standards (AS1100) for technical drawing, focusing on scale, line types, and dimensioning conventions for both 2D and 3D representations.

Prac: Students develop a suite of technical drawings for their chosen concept, including orthographic projections and isometric views. They use CAD software to create 3D digital models, exploring how to apply textures and lighting to produce high-quality rendered views for marketing. Students annotate their drawings with technical specifications, material callouts, and assembly details to ensure the design is ready for the production planning phase.

resources.value: CAD Software (e.g., Onshape, Fusion 360), AS1100 drawing standard guides, digital rendering tutorials, technical drawing equipment.

theory.value: Graphical representation serves as the primary language of design, ensuring that manufacturers can interpret and produce a solution exactly as intended. Technical drawings must adhere to strict conventions, such as AS1100, to maintain clarity and universal understanding across global supply chains. Orthographic projection provides a set of 2D views (top, front, side) that are essential for defining dimensions and assembly details. 3D visualisation, through techniques like isometric drawing or digital rendering, is used to represent the form and aesthetic of a product, making it a powerful tool for pitching ideas to non-technical audiences like potential investors.

prac.value: Students work in the CAD lab to build a digital twin of their product, focusing on accurate geometry and part relationships. They produce a set of dimensioned orthographic drawings, ensuring all line weights and symbols comply with Australian Standards. Using the rendering engine within the CAD software, students experiment with different material finishes (e.g., brushed aluminium vs. matte polymer) to visualise the final aesthetic. Detailed annotations are added to describe specific features that cannot be easily drawn, such as surface treatments or internal mechanisms.

assessment.value: Formative assessment of CAD models and orthographic drawings for technical accuracy and adherence to standards.

lessons.title: Principles of Technical Drawing (AS1100)
lessons.learningGoal: Interpret AS1100 standards for technical drawing to ensure clear graphical communication of product geometry.

orientate.smartStart: Examine the sample technical drawing projected on the whiteboard and write down the names of the 3 distinct line types displayed (continuous thick line, dashed thin line, and thin chain line).

activities.title: AS1100 Terminology Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach AS1100 as the mandatory Australian visual grammar bridging commercial design and mass fabrication. Detail how ambiguous drawings cause catastrophic manufacturing tolerances and financial waste. Model mapping definitions to terms: 'When identifying Orthographic Projection, examine the definition bank for orthogonal 2D planes that describe 3D forms.' Guide students through the layout of the table.
activities.studentsDo: Read each term in the first column and select the matching standard definition from the definition bank, recording the correct text or letter in the Match column of your workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each AS1100 technical drawing term to its correct definition from the bank by writing the corresponding statement in the Match column.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is a standardised graphical language such as AS1100 essential when sending digital designs to an offshore manufacturer?
Expected: It eliminates linguistic barriers and misinterpretations of geometry, scale, and tolerances across global supply chains.
question: What physical manufacturing error occurs if scale is omitted from a technical drawing?
Expected: Fabricators may construct the product to an arbitrary physical dimension or fail to allocate correct tooling tolerances, causing component assembly failure.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions to master: Scale (the fixed numerical ratio between drawing units and physical product size); Orthographic Projection (multiview 2D orthogonal representation of a 3D geometry); Dimension Line (fine continuous line terminated by arrowheads establishing spatial extent).
activities.eLearning: Project the AS1100 reference chart on the main screen; conduct rear-of-room monitoring while students complete vocabulary matching in their workbooks.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students that we are moving from individual definitions to the structural logic of orthogonal views. Direct students to prepare for the next activity.

workbookSpec.title: AS1100 Terminology Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Match each technical term to its authoritative AS1100 definition from the bank.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Scale: A | Orthographic Projection: B | Dimension Line: C
bank: A) The fixed ratio of a drawing's linear dimensions to the actual physical dimensions of the manufactured object.
B) A system of representing 3D objects using multiple 2D views projected orthogonally across perpendicular planes.
C) A thin continuous line terminated by distinct arrowheads that indicates the exact extent and direction of a measurement.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Scale: A (The fixed ratio of a drawing's linear dimensions to the actual physical dimensions of the manufactured object.)
Orthographic Projection: B (A system of representing 3D objects using multiple 2D views projected orthogonally across perpendicular planes.)
Dimension Line: C (A thin continuous line terminated by distinct arrowheads that indicates the exact extent and direction of a measurement.)

activities.title: Fundamentals of Orthographic Projection
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the glass-box theory of third-angle orthographic projection using a physical timber mounting bracket. Model projecting alignment lines from the Front (Elevation) view horizontally to establish the Side (End) view, and vertically to establish the Top (Plan) view. Emphasise that projection lines guarantee dimensional consistency between separate 2D views without re-measuring.
activities.studentsDo: Track the teacher's whiteboard demonstration and complete the cloze passage by selecting appropriate technical terms from the word bank to consolidate projection rules.
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill in the numbered blanks in your cloze passage using the exact technical terms provided in the word bank.
activities.questioning:
q: Why can an industrial manufacturer not fabricate a complex commercial housing from an isometric view alone?
Expected: Isometric drawings contain optical foreshortening and cannot display internal hidden features or true geometric planar dimensions simultaneously.
q: Which view is always selected as the Front view under AS1100 guidelines?
Expected: The view that displays the most characteristic contour, primary functionality, and longest major dimension of the product.
activities.scaffolding: Projection Rules: 1. Front view defines height and length; 2. Top view directly aligns above front view defining length and depth; 3. Side view directly aligns horizontally defining height and depth; 4. Continuous projection lines ensure 100% alignment.
activities.eLearning: Display an animated 3D glass box unfolding into a standard 2D third-angle orthographic layout on the interactive panel.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students: 2 minutes remaining on notes before we apply our knowledge to interrogate a commercial technical drawing for AS1100 compliance.

activities.title: Technical Drawing Defect Identification
activities.teacherDoes: Project the 'Sample Orthographic Bracket Drawing' containing three intentional AS1100 violations and one correct feature. Model interrogating callout 1: 'Notice callout 1 points to a solid continuous line where an internal bore exists. Under AS1100, internal non-visible edges must be rendered using dashed thin hidden detail lines.' Guide students to analyse the remaining callouts independently.
activities.studentsDo: Analyse the numbered callouts on the projected technical drawing and write the specific AS1100 line type or dimensioning violation beside each callout number in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine callouts 1 to 4 on the projected technical drawing. In your workbook, record the specific line type or dimensioning error for each numbered callout using AS1100 conventions.
activities.questioning: Why must centre lines project past the perimeter of a cylindrical hole rather than ending flush with the circle edge? Expected: To clearly show the axis of symmetry and indicate that the feature is a circular hole or revolved geometry rather than a flat cutout. What occurs if dimension lines cross extension lines on a production sheet? Expected: It creates visual confusion, making it difficult for machine operators to distinguish between the physical part profile and measurement boundaries.
activities.scaffolding: AS1100 Line Conventions: Hidden detail = dashed thin line; Centre line = long dash, short dash chain; Dimension line = continuous thin with closed filled arrowheads; Visible outline = continuous thick line (0.5mm).
activities.eLearning: Freeze the high-resolution annotated bracket drawing on the projector screen for students to inspect.
activities.transition: Direct students to set pens down and review the Smart Finish prompt on the board.

workbookSpec.title: AS1100 Technical Drawing Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate the four numbered callouts on the orthographic drawing figure and explain the standard or error represented.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Callout 1: Violation - Solid continuous line used for internal bore hole; AS1100 requires a dashed thin hidden detail line. Callout 2: Violation - Dimension line intersects extension line; AS1100 requires shorter dimensions placed closer to the object and longer overall dimensions placed further out. Callout 3: Violation - Centre line omitted from hole axis; AS1100 requires a thin long chain line (long dash, short dash) extending past the hole perimeter. Callout 4: Compliant - Dimension text placed clearly above and aligned with an unbroken continuous dimension line outside the object profile.
workbookSpec.figureHint: Orthographic projection of a commercial mounting bracket containing deliberate AS1100 errors: solid line used for internal bore, intersecting dimension lines, missing centre line, and correct external dimension.

activities.title: CAD Workspace and Parametric Feature Creation
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate launching the CAD application, establishing a new Part Studio, and anchoring a sketch to the global origin datum. Explicitly model: 'Notice that without constraining my initial sketch to the origin, the geometry remains blue and unconstrained, meaning dimensions can float. Once I lock it to the origin and dimension to 120mm by 60mm, it turns black and fully constrained. Next, I execute a 25mm blind extrusion.' Walk through the 4 core workspace zones and model labelling them on the wireframe template.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher's modelled workflow. On the CAD interface wireframe template in your workbook, label the 4 critical software interface zones and write the function of each zone.
activities.visibleInstructions: Label the 4 key regions on your CAD interface diagram: Tool Ribbon, Feature Tree, 3D Graphics Viewport, and View Cube. Note the primary function of each.
activities.questioning:
q: Why is it vital to fully constrain a 2D sketch to the origin before executing an extrusion?
Expected: Unconstrained sketches can shift unexpectedly when downstream features or assembly mates are modified, corrupting parametric geometry.
q: What is the functional role of the Feature Tree during digital twin development?
Expected: It maintains a chronological, editable history of parametric operations, allowing designers to alter historical dimensions or suppress features.
activities.scaffolding: Parametric Workflow: 1. Plane Selection (Top/Front/Right); 2. Create Sketch profile; 3. Geometric Constraints (Coincident to Origin, Horizontal, Vertical); 4. Dimensional Constraints (Exact mm); 5. Feature Execution (Extrude/Revolve).

workbookSpec.title: CAD Workspace Architecture
workbookSpec.prompt: Label the 4 functional regions of the CAD user interface and describe their role in parametric modelling.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
1. Tool Ribbon: Houses primary 2D drawing and 3D solid modelling commands.
2. Feature Tree: Displays chronological sequence of sketches and features.
3. Viewport: Central interactive space where 3D geometry is visualised.
4. View Cube: Manages camera projection modes and view orientations.

regions.label: Sketch and Feature Tool Ribbon (Top Bar)
View Cube and Camera Navigation (Top Right)

activities.workbookMaterials: Workbook wireframe diagram: CAD Workspace Architecture
activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. Sketch and Feature Tool Ribbon: Houses primary 2D drawing and 3D solid modelling commands (Sketch, Extrude, Fillet, Shell).
2. Browser / Feature History Tree: Displays chronological sequence of sketches and features; allows parametric editing and roll-back.
3. 3D Graphics Viewport and Origin Datum: Central interactive space where 3D geometry is visualised, manipulated, and aligned to axes.
4. View Cube and Camera Navigation: Manages camera projection modes (isometric/orthographic) and view orientations (Top, Front, Right).

activities.title: Guided Component Refinement: Fillets, Shells, and Storyboarding
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through transforming raw geometry into a realistic commercial housing. Lead the class through executing an internal Shell command (2.5mm wall thickness) to simulate injection-moulded plastic, followed by applying 3mm structural fillets to exterior edges. Model: 'Applying a fillet reduces stress concentrations at 90-degree internal corners, preventing premature fracture during commercial impact testing.' Guide students to record this progression across their 4 storyboard frames.
activities.studentsDo: Apply the shell and fillet commands to your personal CAD concept in lockstep with the teacher. Sketch and document each technical milestone across the 4 frames of your Component Evolution Storyboard.
activities.visibleInstructions: Follow the live CAD steps: apply a 2.5mm shell and 3mm exterior edge fillets. In your workbook storyboard, sketch and describe the product state at each of the 4 development stages.
activities.questioning:
q: How does executing a Shell command transform a digital model into an authentic digital twin for manufacturing?
Expected: It converts a solid billet into a hollow component with uniform wall thickness, reflecting actual injection moulding or casting production realities.
q: Why does commercial product design require fillets on external edges?
Expected: It improves consumer ergonomics, reduces stress concentrations, and facilitates smooth part ejection from steel moulds.
activities.scaffolding: Manufacturing Parameters: Wall thickness for ABS/Polymer = 2.0mm–3.0mm; External fillet radius = 3.0mm; Draft angle considerations = 1–2 degrees for mould release.
activities.eLearning: Conduct rear-of-room monitoring using teacher workstation dashboard to verify student geometry constraints and resolve broken sketch loops.

activities.title: AS1100 Annotation and Dimensioning Rules
activities.teacherDoes: Model the generation of a 2D drawing sheet directly from a 3D digital twin in the CAD software. Demonstrate AS1100 rules: 1. Placing overall dimensions furthest from the view and individual feature dimensions closest; 2. Maintaining an 8mm offset between dimension lines; 3. Adding leader lines with sharp arrowheads touching the feature for material specifications. Model: 'Observe how I place the text centrally above the dimension line so it is legible from the bottom or right edge of the drawing sheet.' Guide students through auditing these rules on the workbook table.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher's modelled drawing setup. Review the sample bracket drawing provided on the board and complete the AS1100 audit table in your workbook by checking compliant features and noting necessary corrections.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the AS1100 Drawing Audit table in your workbook. Tick whether each dimensioning rule is compliant on the sample drawing and record corrective actions in the Notes column.
activities.questioning:
q: Why does AS1100 dictate that smaller feature dimensions must sit inside larger overall dimensions?
Expected: To prevent extension lines from crossing dimension lines, which causes visual clutter and misreading of tolerances.
q: How should a material specification callout be positioned relative to the component?
Expected: Outside the component profile, pointing directly to the target surface via an inclined leader line with an arrowhead, with horizontal text.
activities.scaffolding: AS1100 Golden Rules: 1. Dimensions outside the view outline; 2. No intersecting dimension lines; 3. Text readable from bottom or right; 4. Leader lines angled between 30–60 degrees terminating in arrowheads; 5. Units in millimetres (mm) without printing 'mm' on each number.

keyTeachingExperiences.value:
Theory: Analysis of project management frameworks used in the design and manufacturing industries to ensure efficiency and quality control. Students learn about Critical Path Analysis (CPA) and how to sequence manufacturing tasks to minimise downtime. The lesson covers risk mitigation strategies, focusing on identifying potential production bottlenecks and safety hazards before they occur in the workshop.

Prac: Students use digital tools to develop a comprehensive project management plan, including a detailed Gantt chart. They create a sequenced production plan that lists all tools, processes, and materials required for each stage of the build. Students set time-based performance indicators (KPIs) to track their progress and document safety procedures for the high-risk equipment they intend to use during production.

resources.value: Gantt chart software (e.g., ClickUp, Excel), production plan templates, workshop safety manuals, current material price lists.

theory.value: Effective project management in a commercial context is about balancing scope, time, and cost to deliver a high-quality product. Critical Path Analysis helps designers identify the longest sequence of dependent tasks, showing which activities must be completed on time to avoid delaying the entire project. Resource sequencing involves planning the order of operations—such as cutting, shaping, and finishing—to optimise workshop flow and reduce material waste. Risk management plans identify potential issues, such as equipment failure or material shortages, and establish contingency steps to keep production on track.

prac.value: Students use project management software to break their product down into individual components and associated manufacturing tasks. They estimate the time required for each process and input these into a Gantt chart to visualise the overall production schedule. Working in the workshop environment, they conduct a 'Safety Audit' of the tools they will use, creating a risk assessment for their specific project. They also develop a Bill of Materials (BOM) that includes current market costs to ensure their production plan remains within the hypothetical budget.

assessment.value: Formative evaluation of the Project Management Plan (Gantt chart and Production Sequence) and Safety Risk Assessment.

activities.title: Project Management Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the core project management terminology. Model how a bottleneck in a manufacturing cell creates an immediate financial penalty due to idle labour and machinery. Script: 'In commercial production, time is capital. When we map a critical path, we determine the sequence of dependent tasks that cannot slip by even an hour without pushing back the client delivery date. Look at the four definitions in your bank and match each to its term.'
activities.studentsDo: Read the scaffolded definition bank in the workbook. Write the matching definition next to each locked project management term.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Read the four definitions in the bank. 2. Write the matching definition beside each locked term in the table. 3. Check that all four rows are complete.
activities.questioning: Why does a delay in a critical path task force an extension of the entire project deadline? Expected: Tasks on the critical path have zero float; because downstream tasks depend directly on their completion, any delay pushes back the final handover date. How does identifying a potential bottleneck serve as proactive risk mitigation? Expected: It highlights where machinery or labour constraints will cause queues, allowing the manager to allocate extra capacity or adjust sequencing before fabrication begins.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
- Critical Path: The longest continuous chain of dependent tasks that dictates the minimum project duration.
- Bottleneck: A process stage or machine where capacity is lower than demand, causing production backlogs.
- Slack/Float: The duration a non-critical task can be delayed without shifting the overall project completion date.
- Milestone: A critical checkpoint or major deliverable marking the conclusion of a key production stage.
activities.eLearning: Project the definitions on the main screen for 4 minutes during direct instruction, then switch to the live whiteboard prompt.

activities.title: Hierarchy of Controls Deconstruction
activities.teacherDoes: Deconstruct the Hierarchy of Controls using the workshop bandsaw as a worked exemplar. Script: 'A hazard is an object or situation with the potential to cause harm; risk is the probability and severity of that harm occurring. When we assess a bandsaw, the exposed moving blade is the hazard. Elimination means removing the machine entirely. Substitution means using a handsaw. Engineering means fitting an adjustable blade guard and interlocking switch. PPE is merely safety glasses. Notice that engineering controls physically block the hazard, whereas PPE only minimises the injury after contact happens.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the modelled bandsaw analysis. Review the Hierarchy of Controls definitions in the bank and match each control level to its operational description in the table.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Match each level of the Hierarchy of Controls in column 1 to its description in the bank.
2. Write the matching description in column 2.
3. Ensure all six levels are paired accurately.
activities.questioning:
Why are engineering controls considered superior to administrative controls and PPE?
Expected: Engineering controls physically isolate the hazard from the operator independently of human compliance, whereas administrative controls and PPE rely entirely on operator behaviour.

In what scenario would substitution be applied in our prototype workshop?
Expected: Replacing solvent-based aerosol spray paint with water-based brush-on acrylic to eliminate toxic vapour and flammability risks.
activities.scaffolding:
Hierarchy of Controls (Ranked Most to Least Effective):
1. Elimination: Completely remove the hazard from the workspace.
2. Substitution: Replace the tool or chemical with a safer alternative.
3. Isolation: Physically enclose the hazard away from operators.
4. Engineering: Install mechanical guards, extraction, or emergency shut-offs.
5. Administrative: Establish Safe Operating Procedures (SOPs), signage, and operator training.
6. PPE: Equip operators with personal protective gear (safety glasses, ear protection, closed-toe boots).
activities.eLearning: None; teacher delivers focused physical modeling at the workshop demonstration bench.

workbookSpec.title: Hierarchy of Controls Classification
bank: Physically remove the hazard entirely from the workplace.
Replace the dangerous material or process with a safer one.
Physically separate the person from the source of danger.
Install physical guards, interlocks, or extraction systems.
Implement training, safe work signage, and operating procedures.
Personal protective equipment worn as a final barrier to injury.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Elimination: Physically remove the hazard entirely from the workplace.
Substitution: Replace the dangerous material or process with a safer one.
Isolation: Physically separate the person from the source of danger.
Engineering: Install physical guards, interlocks, or extraction systems.
Administrative: Implement training, safe work signage, and operating procedures.
PPE: Personal protective equipment worn as a final barrier to injury.

activities.title: Co-constructing High-Risk Equipment Mitigations
activities.teacherDoes: Guide the class through auditing three standard workshop machines: the Pedestal Drill, Disc Sander, and Compound Mitre Saw. Model the correct professional terminology by explicitly stating the mechanical hazards and the corresponding Hierarchy of Controls level (Elimination, Substitution, Engineering, Administrative, PPE). For example, state: 'For the pedestal drill, a rotating spindle presents an entanglement hazard. While safety glasses address eye strikes, our primary engineering control must be the interlocked guard and our administrative control must be mandatory apron and hair-net compliance.' Ensure students record precise technical descriptions rather than generic statements.
activities.studentsDo: Collaborate in pairs to complete the equipment risk register in the workbook. Document the specific mechanical hazard for each tool and write verified control strategies that specify the hierarchy level.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Review the three workshop tools listed in your table. 2. For each tool, record the primary mechanical or physical hazard. 3. Detail a higher-order control strategy combining Engineering and Administrative controls, and explicitly identify the hierarchy level.
activities.questioning:
question: If a student wears safety glasses at the pedestal drill, does that control the entanglement hazard of loose hair or drawstrings?
expected: No; safety glasses only protect against flying chips or projectiles. Entanglement requires administrative controls such as hair tied back and clothing secured, alongside engineering chuck guards.
question: What engineering control exists on the disc sander to prevent timber jamming and user laceration against the abrasive face?
expected: The adjustable work rest table set strictly within 2mm of the abrasive face, preventing material from wedging between the table and the moving belt or disc.
activities.scaffolding:
Equipment Audit Stems:
- Pedestal Drill: Hazard = Rotating chuck entanglement / projectile swarf. Primary Control = Engineering (Interlocked safety shield) + Admin (Hair tied back, SOP training).
- Disc Sander: Hazard = Timber kickback / skin abrasion / dust inhalation. Primary Control = Engineering (2mm table gap adjustment & dust extraction).
- Mitre Saw: Hazard = Blade laceration / projectile offcuts. Primary Control = Engineering (Retractable guard & hold-down clamp).
Hierarchy of Controls Reference: Elimination -> Substitution -> Engineering -> Administrative -> PPE.

activities.title: Gantt Logic and Scheduling Fundamentals
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly demonstrate how to construct a Gantt chart for a manufactured product. Model the relationship between predecessors, duration, and dependencies on the board. Script: 'A Gantt chart is not merely a calendar; it is a mathematical model of project flow. Look at Task 3: Fabrication. It has a predecessor of Task 2: Material Procurement. You cannot cut stock that has not been delivered. If material sourcing is delayed by 3 days, fabrication is pushed by 3 days. Because fabrication sits on the critical path, the entire handover date moves by 3 days.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher modeling of predecessor links. Complete the cloze notes in the workbook to capture key production planning terminology.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Watch the scheduling demonstration. 2. Select the correct terms from the word bank to fill blanks 1 to 5. 3. Verify each term's role in production planning.
activities.questioning: What distinguishes a milestone from a standard task in a Gantt chart? Expected: A milestone has zero duration and marks the completion of a major phase, whereas a task represents work performed over a set duration. Why must material procurement always precede fabrication in your project timeline? Expected: Fabrication has a mandatory dependency on raw material availability; without the physical substrate, fabrication cannot initiate.
activities.scaffolding:
Key Scheduling Terms:
- Gantt Chart: Visual horizontal bar chart illustrating project schedule, dependencies, and progress.
- Duration: The total working time required to complete a specific task.
- Dependency: A relationship where a successor task cannot begin until its predecessor finishes.
- Bill of Materials (BOM): Comprehensive itemised listing of all raw materials, hardware, quantities, and costs.
- Critical Path: The sequential chain of tasks with zero float determining the minimum build time.

keyTeachingExperiences.value:
Theory: Exploration of iterative design principles, focusing on how rapid prototyping allows for the early detection of functional and ergonomic issues. Students distinguish between additive (3D printing) and subtractive (laser cutting, CNC) prototyping technologies. Discussion centres on the 'Fail Fast, Fail Cheap' philosophy, emphasizing how low-fidelity models reduce overall project risk and improve the final user experience.

Prac: Students produce low-fidelity physical models using rapid prototyping materials like cardboard, foam, or 3D printed components. They conduct initial user testing with these models to gather feedback on scale, comfort, and basic functionality. Every modification made to the design is documented in their digital journal, showing the evolution from the initial CAD model to a refined prototype based on testing evidence.

resources.value: 3D printers, laser cutter, prototyping foam, hot glue, digital journal templates, user feedback forms.

theory.value: Iterative design is a cyclic process of prototyping, testing, analysing, and refining a solution until it meets the performance criteria. Rapid prototyping techniques, such as 3D printing and laser cutting, enable designers to create physical representations of digital designs in hours rather than days. Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer, allowing for complex geometries that are impossible with traditional methods, while subtractive manufacturing removes material from a solid block. The goal of early-stage prototyping is to validate assumptions about the user interface and mechanical function before committing to expensive final materials.

prac.value: Students use the laser cutter or 3D printers to create 'form-study' prototypes of their project's key components. They participate in a 'Testing Carousel' where peers provide feedback on the ergonomics and intuitive use of the prototypes. Based on this feedback, students return to their CAD models to make necessary adjustments to dimensions or fastener locations. All iterations are photographed and annotated, explaining the specific design problem identified and how the subsequent modification aims to resolve it.

assessment.value: Formative feedback on iterative design documentation and the quality of the low-fidelity prototypes.

activities.title: Core Prototyping Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the four core vocabulary terms using physical artefacts: hold up a fused deposition modelling (FDM) 3D print to illustrate additive manufacturing (layer-upon-layer accumulation), and a laser-cut acrylic plate to illustrate subtractive manufacturing (selective material removal). Define iterative design as an ongoing feedback loop of prototyping, testing, analysing, and refining. Explain that a low-fidelity prototype uses inexpensive materials to evaluate scale, ergonomics, and spatial form before committing capital to tooling.
activities.studentsDo: In your workbook, match each locked prototyping term in column 1 to its correct technical definition from the bank by writing the matching letter in the Match column.
activities.visibleInstructions: Review the definition bank in your workbook. Write the correct letter in the Match column next to each technical term.
activities.questioning: Why can additive manufacturing create complex enclosed internal channels that subtractive CNC machining cannot? Expected: Additive processes construct geometry layer-by-layer from the base up, whereas subtractive cutter heads require direct physical line-of-sight and tool access to remove material. How does testing an early low-fidelity prototype reduce commercial financial risk? Expected: Flaws in ergonomics or scale are discovered when using cheap materials such as card or foam, avoiding thousands of dollars in lost tooling or re-machining costs.
activities.scaffolding:
Iterative Design: A cyclic process of prototyping, testing, analysing, and refining a solution until it satisfies all functional criteria.
Additive Manufacturing: A fabrication technology that creates physical components layer-upon-layer directly from digital geometry (e.g. 3D printing).
Subtractive Manufacturing: A fabrication technology that shapes parts by progressively cutting away material from a solid block or sheet (e.g. laser cutting, CNC routing).
Low-Fidelity Prototype: A fast, low-cost physical representation used to evaluate ergonomics, scale, and assembly without incurring production tooling expenses.
activities.eLearning: Laptops closed and resting flat on desks during the physical artefact demonstration.
activities.transition: Now that we have locked down our four core technical terms, let us examine how these concepts connect within the practical iterative engineering cycle.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. Low-Fidelity: Material cost under $2.00, iteration turnaround in minutes; errors in scale or bolt-hole alignment can be corrected immediately with a blade and adhesive without financial loss.

activities.title: Scoring and Cutting Fabrication Techniques
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the precise physical techniques for card and foam prototyping at the central demonstration bench. Show scoring technique: holding the steel safety ruler firmly with fingers behind the guard, orient the utility blade at 45 degrees, applying light pressure to slice only the top liner of corrugated cardboard to form a clean, structural 90-degree bend. Contrast this with a full shear cut where firm, vertical pressure slices through all layers onto the cutting mat. Emphasise how internal fluting gives rigidity and how hot glue must be applied sparingly along internal seams to preserve true exterior dimensions.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration from around the bench. In your workbook, annotate the provided net diagram by labelling the four callouts with the correct fabrication technique and purpose.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the bench demonstration. Complete callouts 1 to 4 on your workbook net diagram, identifying scoring lines, shear cuts, ergonomic grip zones, and glue seams.
activities.questioning: Why do we score the exterior face of corrugated card rather than cutting straight through when creating a clean corner? Expected: Scoring cuts only the outer paper liner, allowing the inner fluting and bottom liner to fold cleanly without separating the two faces, maintaining structural stiffness. Why must adhesive be kept strictly to the internal seam rather than smeared on external faces? Expected: External glue build-up distorts outer dimensions and creates false tactile surfaces during ergonomic grip testing.
activities.scaffolding:
Callout Reference Points:
1. Scored Hinge Line: Partial-depth cut through outer liner only; allows 90-degree fold without tearing.
2. Shear Cut Edge: Full-depth vertical cut separating the part from sheet stock.
3. Ergonomic Touch-Point: Region where human fingers or palm grip the chassis.
4. Assembly Seam: Internal tab where adhesive is applied out of sight.
activities.eLearning: Safety camera or visualiser linked to the workshop projector to ensure all students have an unobstructed view of the cutting hand position.
activities.transition: Now that you have annotated the cutting techniques, return to your benches so we can co-construct our workshop safety and quality readiness checklist.

Contrast this with subjective, unhelpful opinions (e.g. 'I don't like the colour').

Expected: Objective feedback measures observable physical interactions and anthropometric dimensions, whereas subjective feedback is based on personal aesthetic preferences.

keyTeachingExperiences.value:
Theory: Investigation into material science fundamentals and how structural integrity is calculated and tested in product design. Students learn about mechanical properties such as tensile strength, compression, and shear, and how these affect a product's durability under load. The lesson also explores the ethical implications of material durability vs. planned obsolescence in commercial product lifecycles.

Prac: Students design and conduct controlled tests on material samples or prototype joints to evaluate their strength and suitability. They use testing apparatus to apply loads and record the point of failure, documenting the results in a technical report. This data is used to justify the final material thicknesses and joining methods selected for the summative Shark Tank build.

resources.value: Force gauges, weights, material samples (timbers, polymers, metals), data logging software, stress/strain charts.

theory.value: Structural integrity ensures that a product can withstand the forces it will encounter during normal use without failing. Designers must understand the relationship between stress (force applied) and strain (deformation) to select materials that offer an appropriate safety factor. Durability is not just about strength; it also involves resistance to wear, corrosion, and environmental degradation over time. Ethical design necessitates selecting materials that offer a long service life, reducing waste and the environmental impact associated with frequent product replacement and disposal.

prac.value: Students set up a testing station in the workshop to perform comparative stress tests on different joining methods (e.g., mechanical fasteners vs. adhesives). They use weights or force gauges to determine the breaking point of their prototype components, recording the data in spreadsheets. Students then analyse these results to create 'Material Data Sheets' for their project, justifying why their selected materials will ensure the product's commercial longevity. These findings are used to refine the final technical drawings before the final production phase begins.

assessment.value: Formative submission of the Material Testing Report and justified material selection data.

lessons.title: Material Science & Structural Forces
lessons.learningGoal: Analyse the structural forces of tension, compression, and shear acting on product materials and explain their impact on structural integrity.

orientate.smartStart: Complete the quick retrieval challenge in your workbook: Identify three common commercial products and state the primary mechanical force (tension, compression, or shear) acting at their most common point of failure.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can analyse how physical forces act on product materials and explain how this impacts their structural integrity

activities.title: Defining Mechanical Properties & Structural Forces
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the physical definitions of tension, compression, shear, and structural integrity using tactile foam models under load. Demonstrate on the whiteboard how tension stretches outer fibres while compression compacts inner fibres during beam deflection. Model matching the first term 'Tension' with its corresponding physical definition from the bank.
activities.studentsDo: Match each structural force or term in column 1 with its correct definition from the bank by writing the matching definition in the blank cell.
activities.visibleInstructions: Review the force definitions displayed. In your workbook table, match each structural force or term in column 1 to its exact definition from the definition bank provided.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why does a cantilevered diving board experience both tension and compression simultaneously?
Expected: The top surface lengthens under tensile stress while the bottom surface is squeezed under compressive stress.
prompt: What occurs to a material at the microscopic level when subjected to severe shear force?
Expected: Molecular planes slide parallel to each other in opposite directions until structural bonds rupture.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions provided on board:
- Tension: A pulling or stretching force that acts to lengthen a material.
- Compression: A pushing or squeezing force that acts to shorten or crush a material.
- Shear: Parallel forces acting in opposite directions, causing adjacent planes to slide past one another.
- Structural Integrity: The ability of a product to carry designed functional loads without mechanical failure.
activities.eLearning: Ensure all devices are placed aside during the physical foam demonstration.
activities.transition: Now that we have established precise engineering definitions for these forces, we will examine how engineers graph material behaviour using stress-strain curves.

workbookSpec.title: Mechanical Properties & Forces Matching Matrix
workbookSpec.prompt: Match each structural force or term with its correct physical definition from the bank.
bank: A pulling or stretching force that acts to lengthen a material.
A pushing or squeezing force that acts to shorten or crush a material.
Parallel forces acting in opposite directions, causing adjacent parts of a body to slide relative to each other.
The capacity of a designed product or material to support its structural load without breaking or collapsing.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. Tension = A pulling or stretching force that acts to lengthen a material.
2. Compression = A pushing or squeezing force that acts to shorten or crush a material.
3. Shear = Parallel forces acting in opposite directions, causing adjacent parts of a body to slide relative to each other.
4. Structural Integrity = The capacity of a designed product or material to support its structural load without breaking or collapsing.

activities.title: Interpreting Stress vs. Strain Charts
activities.teacherDoes: Project a standard engineering stress vs. strain graph showing the elastic region, yield point, plastic region, and ultimate tensile strength. Walk through the progression: explain that the initial linear gradient is the elastic region governed by Hooke's Law. Model annotating callout 1 as the Elastic Region, explaining that removing stress here results in complete geometric recovery.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the projected stress-strain curve and annotate each numbered callout in the workbook with its correct mechanical zone and operational definition.
activities.visibleInstructions: Refer to the projected diagram. In your workbook, identify each of the 4 callouts and write the mechanical significance of each phase.
activities.questioning:
q: What distinguishes elastic deformation from plastic deformation in commercial product usability?
Expected: Elastic deformation is temporary and harmless during normal use, whereas plastic deformation represents permanent warping and product failure.
q: How does knowing the yield point prevent catastrophic product failures?
Expected: It defines the safe operating threshold where structural components will not permanently deform under maximum expected working loads.
activities.scaffolding: Term bank: Elastic Region (temporary elongation), Yield Point (threshold of irreversible deformation), Plastic Region (permanent material flow), Ultimate Tensile Strength (peak engineering stress prior to fracture).
activities.transition: With these technical thresholds defined, let us evaluate how commercial designers balance durability against planned obsolescence.

workbookSpec.title: Labeling the Stress-Strain Curve
workbookSpec.prompt: Examine the projected stress-strain curve and annotate the four numbered callouts with the correct mechanical region or point.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Callout 1: Elastic Region — Linear zone where stress is proportional to strain; material returns to original dimensions upon load release. Callout 2: Yield Point — Transition boundary where elastic behaviour ends and permanent microscopic dislocation begins. Callout 3: Plastic Region — Zone of permanent, irreversible deformation under applied stress. Callout 4: Ultimate Tensile Strength — Maximum engineering stress the material can sustain before necking and fracture.
workbookSpec.figureHint: Standard Engineering Stress-Strain Curve showing tensile testing parameters.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Callout 1: Elastic Region — Linear zone where stress is proportional to strain; material returns to original dimensions upon load release.
Callout 2: Yield Point — Transition boundary where elastic behaviour ends and permanent microscopic dislocation begins.
Callout 3: Plastic Region — Zone of permanent, irreversible deformation under applied stress.
Callout 4: Ultimate Tensile Strength — Maximum engineering stress the material can sustain before necking and fracture.

activities.title: Material Durability vs. Planned Obsolescence
activities.teacherDoes: Lead a discussion on commercial material selection trade-offs: low-cost polymers versus durable alloys. Model a balanced comparative paragraph on the board, demonstrating how to justify material choice by weighing initial manufacturing cost against lifecycle sustainability and consumer trust.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the structured written response in your workbook, providing a balanced evaluation of planned obsolescence versus ethical, high-durability product engineering.
activities.visibleInstructions: Write your evaluation in the two allocated sections of your workbook. Address economic production incentives in section 1 and ethical lifecycle obligations in section 2.
activities.questioning:
q: Why do commercial appliance manufacturers frequently select low-grade polymers for internal gears instead of machined brass?
Expected: To lower unit manufacturing costs and deliberately drive replacement cycles through planned obsolescence.
q: How does prioritizing material durability contribute to circular design principles?
Expected: Durable materials resist degradation, permitting prolonged product life, modular repairability, and reduced electronic or solid waste in landfills.
activities.scaffolding:
Sentence starters provided:
- Economic section: 'Commercial manufacturers often utilise lower-durability materials to minimise Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) and stimulate replacement cycles because...'
- Ethical section: 'Conversely, engineering for structural longevity and environmental durability ensures that...'
activities.transition: Let us consolidate these material science fundamentals before we enter the workshop for empirical joint testing next lesson.

workbookSpec.title: Material Durability & Ethical Design
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate the commercial trade-offs between selecting low-cost, disposable materials and high-durability structural materials.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Economic Argument: Lower-durability materials such as standard polystyrene or unreinforced polypropylene drastically decrease initial production tooling and unit assembly costs, enabling lower retail pricing and incentivising repeat consumer purchases. Ethical Argument: Selecting high-durability materials like anodised aluminium or glass-filled nylon maintains structural integrity over decades, significantly reducing municipal landfill burdens, carbon emissions associated with continuous remanufacturing, and consumer exploitation through artificial obsolescence.

lessons.title: Testing Joint Strength & Integrity
lessons.learningGoal: Apply physical stress-testing procedures to compare and evaluate the load capacity of mechanical fasteners versus adhesives.

orientate.smartStart: Examine the two sample lap joints at your workstation: Joint A is bonded with PVA adhesive, Joint B is secured with a steel bolt. In your workbook, predict which joint will fail first under pure tensile shear and justify your hypothesis in one sentence.

activities.title: Workshop Testing Protocol and Apparatus Setup
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the standardized destructive tensile-shear test rig using a timber lap joint clamped into a bench vice with calibrated hanging weights and digital force gauges. Explicitly model zeroing the force gauge, establishing safety clearance zones, applying uniform load increments of 10 N, and recording the precise moment and mode of failure (adhesive delamination vs fastener shear). Modelled example: 'Notice how I zero the digital gauge prior to tightening the clamp; failing to tare this scale introduces a pre-load error that invalidates our peak failure threshold.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the calibration and testing procedure. In your workbook, complete the procedural testing checklist to confirm all safety parameters, apparatus calibrations, and data variables are verified.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the live apparatus demonstration. Complete the testing checklist in your workbook by ticking each procedural and safety checkpoint as it is demonstrated.
activities.questioning:
q: Why must loads be added incrementally at steady intervals rather than dropped suddenly onto the joint rig?
Expected: Dynamic shock loading artificially spikes the instantaneous force, creating inaccurate data that does not represent static tensile shear strength.
q: Why is recording the failure mode just as important as recording the peak failure load?
Expected: Identifying whether the fastener bent, the timber split, or the glue sheared reveals the exact mechanical vulnerability of the assembly.
activities.scaffolding:
Checklist criteria:
1. Personal Protective Equipment (safety glasses secured).
2. Force gauge zeroed and calibrated to Newtons.
3. Material joint clamped securely at 90 degrees without initial deflection.
4. Drop zone clear of personnel with catch bucket positioned.
5. Incremental loading protocol ready in 10 N stages.
activities.eLearning: Station the teacher at the main workshop demonstration bench. Laptops remain stowed away from the physical load-testing area.
activities.transition: Now that the testing protocol and safety checks are clear, let us conduct a guided trial run together on sample Joint 1.

workbookSpec.prompt: Verify and tick each critical calibration and safety stage before executing load tests.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All five checklist items must be ticked prior to initiating live testing: 1. Safety glasses and perimeter verified. 2. Force gauge zeroed. 3. Clamping depth verified. 4. Containment in place. 5. Data log ready.

activities.title: Controlled Joint Load Testing Lab
activities.teacherDoes: Circulate among workshop testing stations. Guide student pairs as they mount Specimen A (PVA glued lap joint) and Specimen B (M4 bolted lap joint). Oversee initial loading stages, ensuring students maintain accurate steady increments. Assist groups in identifying and recording the exact point of yield and catastrophic fracture in Newtons. Model reading the force gauge accurately at the precise moment of failure by calling out load increments clearly.
activities.studentsDo: In assigned lab pairs, position material specimens in the test rig. Incrementally apply load, log the force in Newtons at initial deformation and final failure, and note the physical failure mode in the structured data table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Mount your first joint specimen in the rig. Apply loads incrementally, record the yield and fracture loads in Newtons, and document the failure mode in your workbook table using the provided reference bank.
activities.questioning:
question: What visual evidence indicates that the timber adhesive joint is reaching its yield point?
Expected: Faint cracking sounds, micro-fissuring along the glue line, or localized timber fibre peeling.
question: How did the bolted joint distribute the applied load across the specimen compared to the adhesive?
Expected: The bolt concentrated high shear stress around the perimeter of the drilled hole, whereas the adhesive spread stress across the entire surface area.
activities.scaffolding: Failure Mode Reference Bank: Adhesive shear failure (glue separates cleanly from substrate), Substrate tear-out (timber fibres rip before the glue line fails), Fastener shear (bolt or screw bends or snaps), Bearing failure (hole elongates under concentrated bolt pressure).

activities.title: Comparative Structural Evaluation
activities.teacherDoes: Provide individual guidance as students synthesise their empirical workshop data. Model how to extract specific loading and lifecycle metrics from the practical testing session to populate the comparative organiser. Direct students to contrast the structural benefits unique to adhesives (distributed stress, clean aesthetics) versus mechanical fasteners (high ultimate shear strength, disassembly for maintenance), as well as their shared performance characteristics.
activities.studentsDo: Independently complete the three-section comparative overlap organiser in your workbook, classifying advantages exclusive to adhesives, advantages exclusive to mechanical fasteners, and shared structural traits.
activities.visibleInstructions: Synthesize your lab data. In the workbook organiser, categorise the unique mechanical and commercial advantages of Adhesives Only, Fasteners Only, and Both Methods.
activities.questioning:
q: Why might a designer choose an adhesive joint even if its ultimate failure load is lower than a bolted fastener?
Expected: Adhesives distribute load evenly across surface areas without drilling stress-concentrating holes, create watertight seals, and improve visual aesthetic without exposed hardware.
q: What makes mechanical fasteners superior for commercial sustainability and circular lifecycles?
Expected: Fasteners allow non-destructive disassembly for repair, part replacement, and end-of-life recycling.
activities.scaffolding: Consider these factors: stress distribution, ease of repair/disassembly, vibration resistance, installation speed, aesthetic finish, resistance to fatigue.

workbookSpec.title: Adhesive vs Mechanical Fastener Comparison
workbookSpec.prompt: Categorise the performance, manufacturing, and lifecycle characteristics of adhesives versus mechanical fasteners.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Adhesives Only: Even stress distribution over surface; no drilled holes causing stress concentrations; watertight sealing; invisible joints. Both: Capable of supporting operational loads; susceptible to shear failure; require precision alignment. Mechanical Fasteners Only: Reversible/demountable assembly; immediate structural strength without curing; high point-load capacity; facilitates modular maintenance.

activities.title: Deconstructing a Commercial Material Data Sheet
activities.teacherDoes: Project an industry-standard technical Material Data Sheet (MDS) for an injection-moulded commercial product. Explain how professional industrial designers translate raw lab data into technical specifications (yield strength, young's modulus, failure load, environmental resistance, safety factor). Model filling the first technical specification row on the board, demonstrating how to compute a Safety Factor using the formula: Ultimate Strength divided by Working Load. For example, if a bracket breaks at 600N and carries a working load of 200N, the safety factor is 3.0.
activities.studentsDo: Examine the modelled technical data sheet projected on the board. Complete the cloze technical summary in your workbook to embed understanding of how safety margins and material properties are calculated.
activities.visibleInstructions: Follow the teacher modeling on the board. Fill in the missing engineering terms in your workbook cloze activity to define the key metrics of a Material Data Sheet.
activities.questioning:
q: If a commercial bracket experiences an operational load of 150 N, and testing proves failure occurs at 450 N, what is the design safety factor?
Expected: A safety factor of 3.0 (450 N divided by 150 N).
q: Why do commercial designers specify safety factors between 1.5 and 3.0 for consumer goods rather than designing for a factor of 10.0?
Expected: Excessive safety factors lead to over-engineered products that are unnecessarily heavy, costly to manufacture, and wasteful in raw materials.
activities.scaffolding: Formula: Safety Factor (SF) = Ultimate Failure Load (N) / Maximum Working Load (N). Definitions provided: Working Load (normal operational force), Safety Margin (excess structural buffer), Yield Point (start of permanent deformation).

keyTeachingExperiences.value:
Theory: Analysis of industrial assembly techniques and the importance of technical refinement in the final production phase. Students examine how manufacturing workflows are optimised for precision and consistency, focusing on the use of jigs and fixtures. Discussion covers the 'Quality Assurance' (QA) process, where final products are checked against the original design specifications to identify any discrepancies.

Prac: Students execute the final assembly of their Shark Tank commercial product, applying high-level fabrication and finishing skills. They conduct precision checks using calipers and squares to ensure the final build matches their technical drawings exactly. Aesthetic refinement is a priority, with students applying appropriate surface finishes (e.g., sanding, painting, or oiling) to ensure the product is market-ready for the upcoming pitch.

resources.value: Workshop machinery (drills, saws, sanders), finishing materials (paints, oils, waxes), precision measuring tools (digital calipers, squares).

theory.value: Technical refinement is the process of moving from a functional prototype to a high-quality finished product that meets commercial standards. Quality assurance involves systematic monitoring and evaluation of the production process to ensure that standards of quality are being met consistently. Jigs and fixtures are custom tools used to hold parts in the correct position, ensuring repeatability and accuracy during complex assembly tasks. Finishing techniques not only enhance the aesthetic appeal of a product but also provide essential protection against moisture, UV damage, and physical wear.

prac.value: Students begin final fabrication, following their sequenced production plans to cut, shape, and join their final materials. They create custom jigs to assist with difficult assembly steps, such as ensuring perfectly square corners or consistent hole spacing. Once assembled, students perform a 'Tolerance Check,' measuring their product against their technical drawings and documenting any deviations. The final lessons of the week are dedicated to surface preparation and the application of professional finishes, ensuring the product's visual appeal matches its functional quality.

assessment.value: Formative monitoring of production skills and workshop safety; progress check on the final product assembly.

Expected: QA designs processes and standards upfront to prevent defects, while QC inspects products afterwards to catch defects.

activities.title: Calipers & Tolerance Checks
activities.teacherDoes:
Demonstrate the operation of digital calipers (external jaws, internal nibs, depth blade). Model measuring three specific prototype features: overall width, internal slot width, and recess depth. Explicitly calculate deviation: Actual - Nominal = Deviation. Show how to record positive or negative deviations in the audit table.

Modelled Example:
Teacher: 'Class, observe the digital display as I close the external jaws on the reference block. The screen reads zero. Now, measuring our prototype base, the nominal drawing specification is 150.00mm, but our digital readout shows 150.45mm. Subtracting target from actual gives us +0.45mm. I record this positive deviation in our audit table.'

prompt: Why are digital calipers preferred over steel rules for quality assurance checks?

prompt: If your measured dimension is 120.45mm against a nominal spec of 120.00mm, what is your deviation and is it positive or negative?

activities.scaffolding:
Formula displayed: Deviation = Measured Size - Target Size.
Caliper protocol:
1. Wipe jaws clean.
2. Close and press Zero.
3. Apply gentle thumb-wheel pressure.
4. Lock thumb screw and read.

keyTeachingExperiences.value:
Theory: Introduction to commercial marketing principles, focusing on how designers communicate innovation and value to a specific target audience. Students explore brand identity, including logo design and visual style, and how these influence consumer perception. Explicit teaching covers the structure of a persuasive pitch, including the 'hook,' the problem-solution narrative, and the financial justification for investment.

Prac: Students draft their pitch decks and marketing materials, ensuring their brand identity is consistent across all visual aids. They participate in pitch rehearsal sessions, where they practice articulating the commercial viability and innovative features of their design. Peer feedback is used to refine their oral presentation skills, focusing on clarity, body language, and the ability to respond to critical questions about their product.

resources.value: Presentation software (PowerPoint, Canva), graphic design tools, pitch structure templates, public speaking guides.

theory.value: Marketing for product design is the process of building a narrative around a solution that resonates with the needs and desires of a target audience. A brand identity is the collection of all elements that a company creates to portray the right image to its consumer, including logos, typography, and colour palettes. Persuasive communication in a commercial 'pitch' environment requires a balance of emotional storytelling and logical data (such as cost-benefit analysis). Successful designers must be able to justify why their product is a 'better' solution than existing alternatives, focusing on unique selling points (USPs) and market readiness.

prac.value: Students use graphic design software to create a logo and visual brand for their product, which is then integrated into a professional pitch deck. They develop a one-minute 'elevator pitch' that clearly defines the problem their product solves and its primary value proposition. In small groups, students take turns presenting their pitch to 'investors' (peers), who use a feedback rubric to score the persuasiveness and clarity of the presentation. They then refine their pitch based on this feedback, preparing the visual aids and final product display for the summative Shark Tank event.

assessment.value: Formative review of pitch decks and branding elements; peer and teacher feedback during rehearsal sessions.

activities.title: Core Branding Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the commercial significance of branding in industrial design. Direct students' attention to the projector displaying visual identity assets from St Brendan's College and Keppel Bay Marina. Explicitly define Brand Identity, Brand Perception, Typography, Visual Consistency, and Unique Selling Point (USP). Model how Keppel Bay Marina's nautical navy and gold palette deliberately targets marine lifestyle consumers.
activities.studentsDo: Read the five branding terms in column 1 of the workbook. Match each term to its exact definition from the bank below the grid by writing the corresponding letter (A, B, C, D, or E) into the blank Match column.
activities.visibleInstructions: Look at the table in your workbook. Match each branding term in Column 1 to its correct definition from the definition bank by writing the matching letter in the Match column.
activities.questioning:
q: Why is brand perception determined by the consumer rather than the designer?
Expected: Because perception is the emotional interpretation and mental association formed by the buyer, which the designer can only influence through visual cues, not directly dictate.
q: How might an aggressive neon colour palette undermine the perception of a medical or safety device?
Expected: It can signal artificiality, hazard, or toy-like cheapness rather than clinical reliability, sterile precision, and safety.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
- Brand Identity: The visible tangible elements (logo, colours, fonts) created by a designer to identify a product.
- Brand Perception: The emotional reaction and mental reputation consumers associate with a brand upon interaction.
- Typography: The style, typeface selection, and arrangement of written letters to project a specific tone.
- Visual Consistency: The uniform application of colours, fonts, and graphical styles across all marketing touchpoints.
- Unique Selling Point (USP): The distinct feature or capability that sets a commercial product apart from competing market alternatives.
activities.eLearning: Project side-by-side branding collateral from Keppel Bay Marina (https://www.keppelbaymarina.com.au/) and St Brendan's College (https://www.stbrendans.qld.edu.au/) on the main screen.

lessons.title: Crafting the Persuasive Pitch
lessons.learningGoal: Construct a persuasive pitch script containing a compelling 'hook,' a clear problem-solution narrative, and an economic justification.

orientate.smartStart: Read the three sample pitch opening lines projected on the board. In your workbook, record which opener (A, B, or C) best grabs investor attention, and write one sentence explaining how it establishes commercial urgency.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can write a persuasive, structured elevator pitch for my commercial product including a hook, problem statement, and cost-benefit analysis

activities.title: I Do: Anatomy of a Persuasive Hook and Narrative
activities.teacherDoes:
Deconstruct a professional commercial pitch script on the main display. Model how to identify and annotate the four structural pillars: 1. The Hook (evocative statistic or visceral question), 2. The Problem Statement (quantified user pain point), 3. The Solution & Value Proposition (engineered functional features), and 4. The Call to Action (concrete capital request). Explain how opening with 'Did you know...' hooks an investor's commercial instincts immediately.

Modelled Example:
Teacher: 'Notice how the first sentence targets a specific pain point immediately. We write in our first callout: 1 is the hook because it deploys a verified regional statistic to immediately establish market relevance.'
activities.studentsDo: Follow the teacher's modelled analysis on the board. Annotate the sample coastal product pitch script in your workbook by completing the four numbered callout spaces with exact structural explanations matching the legend.
activities.visibleInstructions: Read the sample pitch script in your workbook. Use the numbered callout spaces to label and explain the four structural components: 1. Hook, 2. Problem Statement, 3. Solution, and 4. Call to Action.
activities.questioning:
q: Why is leading with personal introductions such as 'Hi, my name is...' less commercially effective than leading with a problem statistic?
Expected: Personal introductions delay engagement and carry no narrative tension, whereas a statistic or problem immediately defines a commercial opportunity.
q: What is the explicit role of the Call to Action (CTA) in a commercial pitch?
Expected: It specifies the exact financial transaction or partnership required to scale the product into the target market.
activities.scaffolding:
Structural Signposts:
- Callout 1 (Hook): 'Did you know that over 40% of coastal tourists...'
- Callout 2 (Problem): 'Every day, visitors to the Capricorn Coast face restricted mobility...'
- Callout 3 (Solution): 'CoastCycle—a solar-powered e-bike hire network...'
- Callout 4 (Call to Action): 'Join us by investing $50,000 for a 15% equity share.'
activities.eLearning: Display the annotated pitch framework on the projector screen while students work in their physical workbooks.
activities.transition: Now that our persuasive narrative structure is clear, we must anchor our emotional hook in rigorous financial data.

activities.title: We Do: Structuring the Financial Justification
activities.teacherDoes: Guide the class in calculating commercial viability metrics on the board for a demonstration product. Define Cost of Goods Sold (COGS), Wholesale Price, Recommended Retail Price (RRP), Gross Profit ($), and Gross Profit Margin (%). Model: If COGS is $15.00 and RRP is $60.00, Gross Profit = $60 - $15 = $45.00; Profit Margin = ($45 / $60) * 100 = 75%. Emphasise that commercial investors require healthy gross margins to absorb retail markups and logistics.
activities.studentsDo: Work through the mock example calculations alongside the teacher, then calculate the Cost of Goods Sold, Wholesale Price, Retail Price, Gross Profit, and Profit Margin percentage for their own Shark Tank product in column 3.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the financial viability table. Check your calculations against the class mock example in column 2, then calculate and record the metrics for your own product in column 3.
activities.questioning:
q: If your manufacturing cost is $20.00, why is retailing the unit at $25.00 considered commercially non-viable?
Expected: A $5.00 margin (20%) is too thin to support retailer wholesale cuts, marketing acquisition costs, packaging, and shipping overheads.
q: How does presenting a clear 65–75% gross profit margin reassure an investor during a Shark Tank pitch?
Expected: It demonstrates scalability, proves production costs have been audited, and shows the business can weather unexpected cost fluctuations.
activities.scaffolding:
Mathematical Formulas Provided:
- Gross Profit ($) = Retail Price ($) - Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) ($)
- Profit Margin (%) = (Gross Profit ($) / Retail Price ($)) * 100
- Wholesale Standard: Typically 50% of RRP to allow retailer margin.
activities.eLearning: Keep the financial calculation formulas displayed on the board. Monitor calculation accuracy across the classroom.
activities.transition: With our financial figures calculated and verified, let us combine narrative persuasion and commercial metrics into your written pitch script.

Student values will vary by product but must show: Gross Profit = RRP - COGS, and Profit Margin = (Gross Profit / RRP) * 100 with realistic pricing.

Expected: It names the engineered feature (e.g. marine-grade stainless latch) that directly stops the recurring failure (e.g. saltwater corrosion) highlighted in the hook. What makes your Call to Action definitive rather than passive? Expected: It states an exact funding requirement and equity percentage or delivery timeline rather than asking generally for support.
activities.scaffolding:
Sentence Scaffolds:
- 1. Hook: 'Have you ever experienced [specific frustration] while trying to [activity]?'
- 2. Problem: 'The reality across our region is that [target users] waste [time/money] because [root cause].'
- 3. Solution: 'To solve this, we designed [Product Name], featuring [key innovation] that delivers [primary benefit].'
- 4. Financials: 'Manufactured for [COGS] and retailing at [RRP], each unit generates a [Margin %] margin.'
- 5. Call to Action: 'Partner with us today with an investment of [Amount] to launch production.'

activities.title: I Do: Presentation Standards and Slide Consistency Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate contrasting presentation styles: first, a defensive stance with rushed speech, eyes glued to notes, and mismatched slides; second, an open, grounded stance with steady eye contact, deliberate 2-second pauses after the hook, and clean slides. Model auditing a pitch deck against Brand Style Guidelines on the projector, checking logo placement, font families, colour consistency, and uncluttered data presentation. Explicitly articulate how visual harmony reinforces commercial viability.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher's delivery modelling. Open their visual slide decks and conduct a rigorous self-audit against the 5 criteria in their workbook checklist, ticking compliant items and noting required corrections for non-compliant slides.
activities.visibleInstructions: Audit your visual slide deck against the 5 standards in your workbook checklist. Tick each requirement that is fully satisfied, and write a quick fix for any unchecked criteria.
activities.questioning:
question: Why does reading directly from presentation slides damage an investor's trust during a pitch?
expected: It signals that the presenter lacks deep mastery of their own product and commercial data, reducing investor confidence.
question: How does inconsistent typography across slides undermine perceived product quality?
expected: It makes the venture look careless and disorganised, raising doubts about manufacturing precision and attention to detail.
activities.scaffolding:
Audit Standards:
1. Typography: Slide titles use the designated Heading font; bullet points use the Body font.
2. Palette: Visual elements use only the Primary, Secondary, and Accent brand colours.
3. Branding: Product logo mark appears crisp and consistently placed.
4. Visual Balance: High-resolution CAD renders or diagrams dominate over text paragraphs.
5. Financial Integrity: RRP, COGS, and profit margin match written workbook calculations exactly.
activities.eLearning: Project good vs bad pitch slide comparisons. Have students audit their own presentation files on laptops. Monitor screens from the rear of the room.
activities.transition: With your visual slides audited and verified, we now transition into structured peer rehearsal rounds.

workbookSpec.title: Pitch Slide Visual Consistency Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate your digital presentation slides against commercial design standards. Tick each criterion that is fully met.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All 5 criteria ticked. Any unchecked items must show a documented correction applied to the deck prior to rehearsal.
items: Slide typography matches the Heading and Body typefaces from the Brand Style Guideline.
Slide colour palette strictly adheres to the Primary, Secondary, and Accent brand colours.
Product logo mark is sharp, unobstructed, and positioned consistently on template slides.
Slides emphasise CAD renders, diagrams, and concise bullet points rather than dense paragraphs.
Financial figures (COGS, RRP, Gross Margin) match prior written calculations exactly.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Students must evaluate their presentation slides honestly. All 5 criteria should either be ticked or accompanied by an immediate correction note (e.g. 'Slide 3 font changed from Montserrat to Inter', 'Colours adjusted to navy and dune palette').

activities.title: We Do: Peer Pitch Rehearsal Rounds
activities.teacherDoes: Assign peer partners and establish rehearsal protocols. Explain the 4 rubric criteria: Hook Impact, Body Language & Delivery, Clarity of Value Proposition, and Commercial Viability. Run an active split-timer on the projector: Round 1 (Student A pitches for 60 seconds, Student B logs scores and written notes for 2 minutes); Round 2 (swap roles). Circulate between pairs to ensure feedback is constructive, precise, and evidence-based. Model a constructive feedback statement for the class: instead of saying 'your slides looked messy', state 'your font size on slide three is too small to read from the back of the room, so increase it to 24pt'.
activities.studentsDo: Partner A presents their 1-minute pitch while Partner B evaluates their performance in the workbook table, scoring each criterion 1 to 5 and writing specific feedback. Partners swap roles at the timer chime.
activities.visibleInstructions: Take turns delivering your 1-minute pitch to your partner. Evaluator: score each criterion from 1 to 5 and write one specific, actionable improvement note in the feedback column.
activities.questioning:
question: If an evaluator gives a score of 2 on 'Clarity of Value Proposition', what specific revision should the presenter make to their script?
expected: They should explicitly name the functional innovation and describe how it eliminates user frustration, rather than using vague buzzwords like 'revolutionary'.
question: How can a presenter use a strategic 2-second pause after their opening hook to improve delivery?
expected: The pause allows the audience to mentally process the statistic and builds anticipation for the solution.
activities.scaffolding:
Scoring Rubric Descriptors:
- 1–2 (Developing): Unclear problem, mumbled delivery, missing financial justification, slides distracting.
- 3–4 (Proficient): Clear problem, steady eye contact, stated COGS and RRP, visually aligned slides.
- 5 (Shark Tank Ready): Compelling hook, commanding posture, precise profit margins, seamless brand consistency.
activities.eLearning: Project a prominent digital countdown timer (60s pitch / 120s feedback). Signal transitions clearly to keep rehearsal pace crisp.
activities.transition: Conclude your rehearsal rounds. Take your workbook rubric back to your desk to construct your feedback integration plan.
